item.title: Leif Wenar’s Bad Criticisms of Effective Altruism
item.description: Is Sam Bankman Fried the person who “most fully lived out [Effective Altruism’s] credo to do the most good with the resources available”
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Do effective altruists need to grow up? Leif Wenar thinks so—and has written as much in a recent edition of The Economist. However, if poor reasoning, assuming one’s conclusion with little in support of it, and downright bizarre argumentation is supposed to be a condition that one ought to outgrow, then it is Wenar, not the EAs, who should grow up.

Effective altruism is a movement of people trying to make the world better effectively. EAs have directed billions to effective charities, enough to save over 300,000 lives, spare 100+ million chickens from a lifetime in a cage, and plenty of other good. Even if you disagree with EAs about philosophy, you should be happy with the effect that EA has had on the world.

Wenar begins his article by snidely dismissing EAs on grounds that we are “the folks who can look at our fractious and bedraggled world and declare, ‘We must save the shrimp?’” You might, at this point, expect some discussion of what the shrimp welfare project does or why concern for shrimp is silly. We get none of this. Instead, Wenar is relying on the audience to agree with him that the idea sounds weird—and thus dismiss it. This is apparently the serious philosophizing that we EAs may one day reach after we hit puberty and outgrow our youthful dogmatism.

Now, is shrimp welfare a silly and crazy idea especially in our “fractious and bedraggled world?” It costs about one dollar to spare 14,000 shrimp from the pain of death. The Shrimp Welfare Project, despite having a tiny budget, has spared more shrimp from potentially intense agony than the number of people alive in the world. A penny given to the shrimp welfare project averts the equivalent of around 140 painful deaths. Is it supposed to be blindingly obvious that you shouldn’t spare a penny to save 140 shrimp, even knowing that they might be capable of suffering?

Call me crazy, but I would expect that if you are chiding others for their youthful unseriousness, you would give some argument for why we shouldn’t spare more plausibly conscious creatures from suffering than there are people on Earth, at a cost less than that of running a local McDonalds. Wenar rightly notes that “early British utilitarians championed human equality, as they campaigned to end slavery and win equal rights for women.” But those ideas seemed weird at the time too.

If you want to make moral progress, you have to think hard about the prejudices that are deeply ingrained in your society. You can’t just dismissively sneer at any counterintuitive moral claim. And in this case, the claim isn’t even counterintuitive. It just sounds a bit funny.

Wenar then spends several paragraphs talking about how little sense EAs have. He claims that in EA “you won’t see…much common sense about how the world works.” There is no argument given for this. Apparently this is another thing that you’re supposed to take to be true because Wenar says it several times. He then says:

My worry is the effective altruists who become too attached to being the hero. One popular EA book, Will MacAskill’s “What We Owe The Future”, tells you that “you can shape the course of history,” and explains how to “structure global society”. But if you check the footnotes on the climate-change charity that the book calls “extremely cost-effective”, you may be surprised by how shaky the book’s guesswork is and how shoddy its research.

Why are we supposed to think these claims aren’t true? Just because they’re in scare quotes? It really is true that you can shape the course of history. Many of the early EAs who were being mocked for making that claim have gone on to shape the course of history. Big chunks of the field of alignment were invented by individual people. As puts it, in an excellent piece lamenting his early errors in writing off EAs on the topic of AI:

Eleven years onward, it is extremely, extremely obvious that I was wrong. I did not take this then-nonexistent technology remotely seriously enough, and the people I met who did take it seriously were able to do incredibly impactful work because of that. Chris Olah more or less founded the field of mechanistic interpretability (and coined the term!) and went on to cofound Anthropic. Amanda Askell is responsible for Claude’s personality and one of the most influential people in AI. Buck Shlegeris founded Redwood Research, perhaps the most interesting center of technical AI safety work outside of a major lab.

Or look further in the past: Norman Borlaug, Stanislav Petrov, Florence Nightingale, and Vasili Arkhipov have all had enormous impacts on history. So have Donald Trump, Elon Musk, and many others in the modern day. The claim Wenar is criticizing is true. At the very least, if you’re arguing that it’s bad enough that EAs believing it means that we have a diabolical savior complex, you’d better at least explain why you think it isn’t right! Otherwise this is just Bulverism.

As it happens, these quotes are also taken out of context. “You Can Shape the Course of History” is the title of a section arguing that history is often “plastic” in the sense that how it turns out isn’t predetermined. For instance, it’s reasonably plausible, as MacAskill argues in his book, that British abolitionism’s success wasn’t inevitable—and was a major part of the global abolition of slavery. There are ways history could have turned out where slavery would continue to be legal and be tolerated to this day. Maybe this thesis is wrong, but it’s hardly evidence of a savior complex. It’s about history being influenceable, not about individuals.

The other quote is even more thoroughly ripped from context. The phrase “structure global society” appears in the sentence “This last point—that we need to structure global society so that cultural evolution guides the world towards better values and better societal structures—highlights an issue facing the design of a morally exploratory world that I’ll call the lock-in paradox.” Will’s saying that cultures that are good at sticking around and gaining dominance will persist, even if they are bad.

This is an important point. The societies that are best morally might not be mimetically adaptive. As a point of comparison, evolution led to lots of needless horrendous suffering, because the traits that are most adaptive aren’t the ones that are morally best. This hardly seems like—as Wenar implies—some plan for planet-wide social engineering.

Wenar then explains why he thinks GiveWell’s estimate of the number of lives their top charities have saved isn’t accurate. He writes:

Or consider the EA poverty-relief charity, GiveWell. Its front-page pitch is that its grants “will save over 340,000 lives” in poor countries. When you dig into GiveWell’s calculations, you’ll see that they omit many negative factors well known to development economists. GiveWell’s numbers also omit actual deaths. For example, a top-rated GiveWell charity that gives out cash in northern Nigeria reported that one of the many armed bandits who confronted its staff killed two people while looking for the cash. Those deaths are not counted as “minus two” in GiveWell’s “total lives saved” calculations, as by the charity’s own cost-effectiveness reasoning they should be.

The 340,000 lives number comes from:

  1. Getting high quality evidence—largely from randomized control trials—about the effectiveness of their top charities.

  2. Using that to figure out the cost per life saved.

  3. Dividing the total amount of money given to each of those top charities by the cost per life saved number to reach a total number of lives saved.

This number is obviously imperfect. Still, it’s pretty good, especially as far as hard-to-ascertain fuzzy analyses of total lives saved from charity aggregators go. In order to argue that this estimate is unreliable, one would need to argue that it’s leaving out some major factors. Finding one case of a recipient being killed by bandits isn’t evidence that there’s any major overestimation going on, just like finding out that one person died in a car accident on the way to a Medicaid appointment wouldn’t be good evidence against the reliability of a study on lives saved from Medicaid.

GiveWell’s number is much likelier to be an underestimate than an overestimate. It only counts GiveWell top charities, not other grants they’ve given out or charities they used to recommend but don’t anymore. So, for instance, it completely ignores GiveWell efforts to speed along the malaria vaccine and benefits of Give Directly and the Schistosomiasis Control Initiative. It also leaves out all sorts of desirable second-order effects—if you save someone’s life, you improve their ability to take care of others, saving even more people.

And GiveWell has written at length about possible sources of overestimation. For example, Wenar has elsewhere talked about the use of malaria nets for fishing. But GiveWell has a detailed analysis of this and found it to be mostly negligible.

So yes, obviously GiveWell’s estimate is imperfect. It fails to consider second-order effects and various rare possibilities. But Wenar has given no reason at all to think that a more complete analysis would give a lower number. Almost certainly it would give a higher number, given that the benefits left out include incredible numbers of lives saved from other charitable efforts and the only harm Wenar named was a one-off bandit attack.

If we took the Wenar approach seriously—throwing out every estimate so long as it doesn’t account for every single anecdote of a person being harmed—then we could never estimate everything. Those trying to estimate the impacts of USAID or Medicare cuts would be hopelessly drowning in anecdotes. This approach is totally unworkable in practice. Thus, it’s clearly an isolated demand for rigor. The fact that we cannot be fully exact in our estimation doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t try to quantify.

Wenar next portentously pronounces, “What effective altruists love is portentous pronouncements.” He then unaccountably declares “What they don’t tend to love is accountability.” Why does he think that? He says that GiveWell “has never published its “lives saved” claim in a peer-reviewed journal, and the people targeted by its grants seem to have few rights to redress if things go badly.” Ironically, GiveWell top charities are some of the only charities that have been comprehensively evaluated in a peer-reviewed journal.

My guess is peer reviewed journals wouldn’t take papers on the impact GiveWell has had. This kind of estimate is too inside-basebally for general publication. Still, GiveWell reports are subject to rigorous scrutiny from many experts prior to publication. There is no more rigorous charity evaluator anywhere in the world. While it would be nice if it was subject to peer review, I don’t think this would substantially increase the scrutiny that it’s subject to.

Next, Wenar continues the weird and uncharitable psychoanalysis from earlier (perhaps he is doing this because of his childhood):

I sometimes wonder whether effective altruists have begun to pronounce so much about the “long-term” future because they know they’ll be dead long before they’re proved wrong.

This is a ridiculous claim. Among other things, many of the claims EAs make about influencing the long-term future route through near-term impact. For instance, several years ago, EAs were saying that AI would be a big deal. The Leif Wenars of the world were laughing at us and suggesting we were presumptuous, naive, tech bros who believe in a supernatural machine God. Now that these people have been proven wrong, they’ve moved on to laughing at us about other things.

Perhaps the most irritating sequence of sentences in the whole article is:

Effective altruism may be ending as a coherent movement. The proponent who most fully lived out its credo to do the most good with the resources available was the crypto whizz-kid Sam Bankman-Fried. He quite logically saw other people as resources to be used, and he’s now serving 25 years in federal prison for fraud. The old EA leaders who clustered around him have been discredited by their consistently bad judgment.

The first claim is false: EA has been growing extremely quickly recently. The second claim is completely ludicrous. Defrauding people out of billions of dollars—an action that obviously risked the collapse of his fortune and EA’s goodwill—wouldn’t pass any kind of remotely sane cost benefit analysis. This is why EA leaders have been clear repeatedly long before SBF: you should not risk doing grossly immoral things, even if you think it will turn out for the best. The track record is very bad. So treating SBF as the person who “most fully lived out its credo to do the most good” is a statement that is so ludicrous as to be discrediting on its own.

As for the claim that EA leaders who clustered around him have been discredited, that claim has the more limited virtue of not being obviously completely absurd. But it still isn’t right. EA leaders were mostly advising Sam on how to spend his money. They did not know the details of crypto-trading. The markets didn’t predict the staggering scale of his fraud either. To demand that people with no technical crypto background advising SBF on how to spend his money would deduce something none of the markets did—that he was committing staggering fraud—is quite unreasonable. Be specific: how should they have known? If the whole market isn’t to blame, what specific insider info should they have had?

Do the effective altruists in AI have good judgment? Anthropic’s recent safety problems are being investigated by groups with close ties to the boss’s EA friends and family. The main author of the moral “constitution” of Anthropic’s Claude has long intellectual and personal involvement in effective altruism.

The reason that most of the groups concerned about AI safety have ties to EA is that EAs worried about AI safety for about ten years before anyone else did. For being early on this problem, EAs should get credit, not condemnation.

Note that aside from vaguely gesturing at the SBF scandal and saying that EAs have overstated a few stats, Wenar has given no argument for thinking EAs have systematically bad judgment. Seems like this would be a more productive feature of the piece than snarky evidence-free psychoanalysis that we speculate about the future so that we can’t be disproved in the near-term.

If Wenar has criticisms of the Anthropic constitution then he should raise those criticisms. Instead, he has suggested that Amanda Askell is tainted in her ability to write good model constitutions by her bad judgment and nefarious ties to EA. Of course, by all accounts, Askell is an extremely gifted and careful philosopher, whatever her “intellectual and personal involvement in effective altruism.” Anthropic’s constitution may be one reason why Anthropic has a better safety record than OpenAI. And if one reads it, it’s abundantly clear that lots of thought went into it.

Wenar ends his piece in the following way:

I tell them to start by living among the people they want to help. Then get deep expertise—and dwell on the human consequences when some brainy scheme goes wrong. For simple life experience, maybe go into local politics. Or mentor a neighbour’s struggling kid.

It’s probably too late for the effective altruists in AI to do any of this. Their movement’s final legacy may indeed be measured in human lives—just not in ways that they ever imagined.

Despite Wenar’s early criticisms about EAs making decisions without having high enough quality data to support them, his life advice is formed in the absence of any data in favor of it. Certainly mentoring a neighbor’s struggling kid is a decent thing to do. But if the suggestion is that EAs are stupid idiots who should do community action instead, then it seems one should present, I don’t know, some reason to think this is comparably effective to EA activities. We get none of that (and there’s abundant contrary evidence).

Wenar closes his piece by claiming that EAs’ mistakes will be measured in human lives. He gives no argument for thinking EA will lead to any lives lost remotely comparable to the number saved. Wenar’s charge is far more plausibly made against the critics of EA. Running flak against a movement that has demonstrably prevented large numbers of innocent children from dying is very likely to lead to more children dying needlessly. If we’re going to tally up lives lost from attempts to make the world better, we might as well start there.

item.title: Giant Dialogues
item.description: Do giants matter in the aggregate more than humans?
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Bloodbottler: I read your piece “Humans Matter in the Aggregate More Than Giants.” That one provoked a big reaction on giant Twitter (as big of a reaction as one can get from the ~80 giants that live in the world). Did you see, even Fleshlumpeater weighed in. Just know that I would absolutely stomp on a billion humans if it would add even one second to a giant’s life.

BFG: I realize that is the common intuition among giants. But really think about those little humans. Yes, they may be small. We may not be able to see their little lives. But there is compelling evidence that they can suffer. They respond to painful stimulus. They respond to painkillers. So I think our intuitions about the moral unimportance of humans are not very reliable.

Bloodbottler: This conclusion is, of course, ridiculous. It’s not that we have failed to appreciate the importance of humans. I like humans well enough. In fact, when I eventually heard of J.B.S. (short, of course, for just bone smash) Haldane’s quip that God “must have an inordinate fondness for humans,” this struck me as clearly false. Humans are wonderful creatures, and so God’s fondness for them is anything but inordinate! But your error is neglecting the inviolability of the giant person.

BFG: Well let us talk more about that inviolability. While there are 8 billion humans, there are only 80 giants. There are about 100 million humans per giant. I calculated that for each passing second of giant life, there are 75 passing hours of human death. That’s just the death bits—ignoring all the other parts. So what is it that explains why a single second of giant life matters more than any amount of human life?

Bloodbottler: Well let me start by saying that anyone arguing that any other species matters more than all giants in the aggregate is an enemy of giants and should be summarily executed.

BFG: But obviously the fact that you’re part of some group doesn’t mean members of that group matter categorically more than members of other groups. We are northern giants with white skin like the pale snow. But we don’t think the southern giants—swarthy though they may be—matter infinitely less. In fact, giants have a long history of ignoring the importance of one another, which we now recognize to be an error. In fact, it wasn’t so long ago that northern and southern giants had to drink from different water fountains. So shouldn’t we at least take seriously the possibility that human interests matter?

Bloodbottler: I will respond substantively, but first let me signal a little bit more.

> be EA
> massive_intellect.jpg
> r/atheism
> “I don’t need a book to be a good person”
> morality from first principles
> assign a conservative pain variable
> “in aggregate humans have more value than giants”

we should keep malcontent turbo-dweebs away from superintelligence.

BFG: My friend, note that I am but a humble giant who doesn’t speak for EA. And the core ideas of EA have nothing to do with this, so let not this taint your assessment of it. To think that you should rescue a giant drowning in a pond, you don’t need to think that all the humans of the world matter more than a giant. Still, it seems like an important conclusion, so I really wish you’d engage with the argument.

Bloodbottler: Fine, you want me to engage with the argument, I’ll tell you your error. You are assuming utilitarianism. By assuming that the welfare of all the humans can outweigh that of a single giant, you are assuming that welfare can aggregate. But that’s simply assuming utilitarianism. And utilitarianism is crazy and evil! It implies that you should harvest one giant to save five other giants.

BFG: I’m not assuming utilitarianism. To think that the welfare of a billion conscious creatures matters more than the welfare of one, you don’t need to be a utilitarian. It is obviously possible to think that without believing you should always do whatever maximizes aggregate welfare.

Bloodbottler: You are assuming erroneously that a bunch of humans can matter more than one giant. But just like no number of dust specks can matter as much as one torture and no number of headaches can matter as much as a giant life, no number of human lives can matter as much as a giant.

BFG: Well, of course, I have my arguments for the conclusion that lots of little pains can be worse than a single major pain. But even if we set those aside, why think that humans can experience only little pains? Certainly they behave as if they’re in a lot of pain. If you watch those up-close videos of the humans when they’re dying of disease, or see how they react when you stomp them to death, so long as you do it slowly, they react like they’re in a lot of pain. Now, I don’t know the exact ratio of pain in giants to pain in humans. But it’s at least not obvious that they only feel a bit of pain, even though our brains are 80,000 times larger. For this reason, even if I were a non-aggregationist, I would still buy that enough humans’ interests could outweigh one giant’s interests.

Not to mention that the other view has pretty implausible results. It implies that a single passing second of giant life matters more than 75 hours of human life. Now, we may treat human life as irrelevant. But really imagine living for 75 full hours as a human. Isn’t it obvious that would matter way more than just one second of your life?

Bloodbottler: Obvious to whom? Certainly that isn’t obvious to me. Whether it’s obvious to most giants is an empirical question. I think any amount of human life matters less than any amount of giant life.

BFG: Really? Can you please try to think vividly about what it’s like to be a human, rather than just writing them off because it’s convenient to do so? Look, I know it might be annoying to have to take efforts not to stomp the little humans to death. But it’s the right thing to do.

Bloodbottler: Yeah, not moved by this stupid argument, sorry.

BFG: Well do you remember when Bonedrinker proposed his famous veil of ignorance thought experiment. The core idea was that you’re supposed to imagine making decisions as if you didn’t know who in society you would be. That way you’d be impartial and count everyone’s interests equally. In such a setup, you’d obviously care mostly about humans, because you’d be almost guaranteed to be one.

Bloodbottler: But you’re assuming that you could have been a human. That’s ridiculous. It’s not like we’re just souls being slotted into a random body.

BFG: No, I’m obviously not assuming that. It’s a thought experiment. You’re supposed to imagine not knowing who you are. So just as you can have thought experiments where you imagine not knowing that the first digit of pi is 3—even though it couldn’t be anything else—you can also imagine thought experiments where you don’t know that you’re you.

Bloodbottler: I simply refuse to include humans from behind the veil of ignorance.

BFG: But if you’d care about them from behind the veil, doesn’t this show that they impartially matter. And isn’t promoting the impartial good at least part of the source of our moral reasons, even if not all of them?

Bloodbottler: Well you’ve assumed utilitarianism again. You’ve talked a lot about the humans experiencing pleasure and pain. But “this is a utilitarian argument of the pre-Millian, Benthamite sort: pains and pleasures do not differ in any qualitative way but are substantively the same and only need to be added up.” And humans living on our world, with severe cognitive defects, have none of the higher pleasures of relationship, knowledge, or anything else.

BFG: I’ve assumed no such thing. As you know, I’m an objective list theorist. I think there’s more to a good life than just pleasure. My argument is and has always been that pleasure and pain are AMONG the things that matter, not that they’re the only things that matter. So then the fact that humans experience more suffering in a day than all the suffering in giant history means that we should take their interests very very seriously.

Bloodbottler: All I’ll say is k3 civ or bust. The humans can come too.

BFG: I feel like you’re not treating this with the seriousness that it deserves. We know that giants have a long history of making serious moral errors. We also know that there is significantly more expected suffering experienced by humans than giants. They differ by many orders of magnitude. So shouldn’t we at least treat this topic seriously, rather than sneering or writing off the other view.

Bloodbottler: (on giant Twitter)

EA rationalist types are really weird about humans.

You say “Elves don’t have subjective consciousness and so can’t feel pain” and they pop into your replies with
“What about humans? Can humans feel pain? Would you step on a human knowing they feel pain?”

Sure.

“You genocidal monster! How can you not care about the human? Do you know mermaids are giant water humans? Would you sacrifice a trillion humans to save one giant?”

Sure.

“Omg you’re even more evil than I already thought you were! How dare you prioritize your own petty hypothetical consciousness for the very real suffering of a trillion humans!”

Sorry, I don’t value humans. Because they’re humans.
An elf doesn’t have moral standing. It’s an elf.

BFG: I don’t think this has ever happened, but do you see why it is annoying to explain why I think what I do at length and to have you respond with extreme confidence, dismissal, and snark, yet not bother to give a counterargument? If we want to make moral progress, if we want to be the kinds of beings that live up to the enlightenment ideals of Bloodcruncher and Headbasher, then we’d better think carefully about our moral practices. If we do not think about the actions we take, then we are doomed to commit the errors of the past. So please, you don’t have to agree, but don’t just immediately write off every argument for why our society’s moral practices are badly in the wrong.

Bloodbottler: So let’s say we grant this premise. What are the practical takeaways?

BFG: Well to start, I’d say we shouldn’t mistreat trillions of humans in giant human farms in order to provide environmentally harmful and overpriced feed to the suffering krakens on the kraken farms. But the more general thing is that once we recognize that humans matter, then we, who will primarily design how the future goes across vast spans, should aim to design one that is good for all sentient beings—humans included!

item.title: Schmotte and Bailey: Pledge
item.description: A common complaint about EA is definitively wrong
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

(This is an important post, so I’d really appreciate if you shared it and restacked it—thanks!)

Friend of the blog writes about the Schmotte and Bailey fallacy. You tell people to do one relatively uncontroversial thing. They claim that you are telling them to do some other far more controversial thing. So, for example, you tell them to make doing good a major life project. They think you’re telling them to be a utilitariany utilitarian who harvests the organs of innocent humans to give them to shrimp.

A common claim is that EA is either utilitarianism or a tautology. Either EA says: maximize welfare all the time at all costs no matter what, or it’s just the trivial claim that you should do good. , after summarizing EA, says:

Who could argue with that! But this summary also invites perhaps the most powerful critique: who could argue with that? That is to say, this sounds like so obvious and general a project that it can hardly denote a specific philosophy or project at all. The immediate response to such a definition, if you’re not particularly impressionable or invested in your status within certain obscure internet communities, should be to point out that this is an utterly banal set of goals that are shared by literally everyone who sincerely tries to act charitably.

The reply is, of course, that EA is a neglected truism. The core EA idea is that you should make doing good as effectively as you can a major life project. It sounds really obvious when you think about it. But almost nobody acts on the idea. Prior to the dawn of EA, almost nobody looked hard into charitable effectiveness. Other organizations that were focused on tallying overhead even mocked us for this!

Most people don’t give much to charity, and if they do, they give to charities that resonate with them rather than ones that are most effective. If you ask most people who give to charity why they think the charity they gave to is the most effective one, they will give you a vaguely confused look.

So here, I will make very clear that I am not Motte and Baileying you. There is a specific thing I think you should do that you probably do not do. That thing is taking the Giving What We Can pledge and giving 10% of your income to effective charities. I think the case for taking the pledge is extremely strong, but almost nobody does it. In this respect, it’s a neglected truism.

You cannot say that EA claims are all trivial when EAs are saying that you should give 10% of your income to effective charities and almost nobody does that. It can’t be that a claim is too obvious and trivial to need stating if almost nobody acts on it, including you.

The pledge is a pledge to give 10% of your income to effective charities. I have taken the pledge (though I give significantly more than 10%). It is very streamlined and efficient. It allows you to keep all your donations in one place, and see whether you’ve donated 10% of your income to effective charities. Taking the pledge also helps convince others to do so. Thus, if you’re going to give 10%, I think you ought to take the pledge.

Why should you give 10%? Well, here is a very plausible moral premise: intense suffering and death are bad. It is bad when a child dies. If you can prevent something very bad from happening without giving up anything of comparable value, then you should do so. This is why you should pull a child from a pond if doing so would ruin your shoes or pull a child from a car-wreck, even if doing so would ruin your fancy watch.

Giving up 10% of your income would likely save at least a life a year. The best charities save lives for about $4,000. So if you give away 10% of your income, depending on your income, you’ll maybe save one life a year and maybe multiple. Think about some child you know. Imagine that child dying. Then imagine that a stranger could prevent them from dying by sacrificing a small portion of their salary.

Shouldn’t the stranger give a small fraction of their salary, so that the child you know can live? If the far away child dying of malaria was your brother, your child, or your cousin, wouldn’t you want a stranger to save them at the cost of just a few thousand dollars? If someone could have saved my life when I was a child, but didn’t do so because it would have been slightly personally costly, that would have seemed bad. So similarly when some far away child is dying, I should help if I can.

Why should you give to effective charities rather than ineffective ones? The answer is that there is strong moral reason to do more good instead of less good. Almost everyone recognizes this in other contexts. If you can either save five people or two from an oncoming train, everybody (save John Taurek) thinks you should save five. If we apply this logic to the charity sector, we end up with the conclusion that you should donate where you can do the most good. This matters a great deal, because the best charities do hundreds or thousands of times more good than the median charity.

Does the fact that some charities appeal to you emotionally mean that you should give to them even if they don’t do the most good? No. Imagine there were five people dying of typhoid and three of lupus. You could either save the five or the three. Would it be reasonable to save the three on grounds that treating lupus resonates with you more emotionally? No, obviously not. Similarly, when deciding which charity you give to, you should give where you think will do the most good, rather than to the place that resonates with you. Preventing death is more important than feeling happy about the particular way you prevented death.

Is this too demanding? Is this like asking you to give up your life to save ten others—which morality could never command? No, because the cost is not extremely large. Remember, I am not saying you should give away all of your money. Maybe you should do that, but that’s not the ask, and that depends on more controversial ethical assumptions. I am saying that you should give away 10% of it. That still leaves you with 90% which is likely much more than average members of your parent’s generation had, and certainly much more than average members of your grandparent’s generation had.

The correlation between money and happiness is real but pretty small. In contrast, the correlation between charitable giving and happiness is pretty large. The best study on the association between money and happiness found “donating to charity had a similar impact on happiness to household income doubling!”

By giving regularly, you can know that you are making a meaningful difference. There are children who would be dead if you’d never lived, but who instead get to live. This makes your life more meaningful. So my guess is that giving is not a cost. Instead, even if you were selfish you should give. I’m very happy generally, and a big part of that is thinking that I’m making a difference with my life.

But even if it did make you a bit less happy, this would be a small price to pay to save lives regularly. Even if you have a 10% reduction in your happiness, you’ll still be one of the wealthiest 1% of people who ever lived, if you’re in the west. You’ll be one of the richest few percent of people in the world. Going from super duper affluent by historical standards to merely super affluent and saving a bunch of extra lives is worth it!

If you’ll still be able to live well and still be richer than almost everyone who has ever lived after making some sacrifice, then it is hardly the kind of debilitating sacrifice that is too demanding for morality to ever demand. If paying a small price is the only way to prevent many children from dying, then you should do that.

Now, there are some other controversial things I think. So, for example, I think that it’s good to donate to help shrimp, because one dollar can spare thousands of shrimp from a horrible fate. But that is a separate view from the view that you should give to effective charities and most people who give to effective charities don’t believe it. Do not say, then, “I am not on board with giving to effective charities because I don’t care about shrimp, and otherwise EA is a tautology.” It’s not a tautology. It says you should do something that you probably don’t do!

So please, you, whoever is reading this, think hard about whether to give 10% of your income to effective charities. Think hard about whether you want to be the kind of person who sacrifices a small fraction of your income to save a bunch of lives. If you take the pledge, standard offer goes: I’ll give you a free paid subscription to this blog.

My guess is that if you take the pledge, you will be happier and more fulfilled. More importantly, many additional children won’t die unnecessarily. If you could see the children suffering from their diseases, you would see how vital this kind of action is and feel empathy for them.

But the fact that you can’t see them doesn’t make any difference to your reasons to help them. It is a betrayal of the principle behind empathy to only help those who we can see vividly enough to feel for. It is wrong to let children die because they’re too far away away to see.

item.title: Effective Altruists Should Grow a Spine
item.description: Your fave is problematic effective altruism
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

has a great post called Your Fave Is Problematic Politics. It begins with a discussion of a dark and wretched place where many go, where the devil and his angels would dwell aionas ton aionon, called Tumblr. Back in the day, there was a popular Tumblr page called “your fave is problematic,” where people dug up dirt about how problematic various celebrities were. The purpose wasn’t to change anyone’s behavior, but just to get them to acknowledge that their fave was problematic.

Ozy makes the point that people do this about politics too. Lots of progressives, before endorsing Kamala Harris, made some weak-sauce mealy-mouthed statement like “ugh, I hate that I’m having to endorse a prosecutor white supremacist war criminal who probably serves at the right hand of Satan, but it’s better than endorsing Trump who definitely is Satan.” Not exactly a ringing endorsement!

Another area where people are way too mealy-mouthed and defensive is in talking about effective altruism.

When defending it, people caveat and hedge and self-flagellate. They talk endlessly in vague terms about how EA has a lot of problems. They say they’re EA adjacent, even though they work on AI safety and donate a bunch of their income to effective charities. They make sure to acknowledge how their fave is problematic. Often people defending EA sound like they ran over your dog and are trying to defend their conduct.

And you don’t have to do that. Here is a better message when it comes to EA: EA is fucking awesome. It has done an incredible amount of good. Hundreds of thousands fewer people are dead because of EAs. Billions of animals have been spared intense suffering. We’ve been right over and over again even when we were being mocked (e.g. about AI). Pick any existential risk: probably a giant chunk of work to avert it is being done by EAs. Can the fact that we’ve saved 300,000+ lives get more covered than a one-off bandit attack?

The EA community is imperfect, but it’s made up mostly of earnest, kind, decent people striving to make the world a better place. People who spend their careers trying to improve the world. People who give away tens of thousands of dollars annually to spare children from horrible diseases. While a lot of public EA advocates are a bit like me—disagreeable philosopher types—the ordinary EA is the kind of person you want to be friends with.

Often the EA public figures are people like , who rose to prominence being the only person being sane on the AI water issue. Masley is the great Satan of a certain subset of Bluesky for pointing out straightforward facts about AI water use. Lots of the sanest commentators on the internet give away 10% of their income to effective charities (e.g. Jesse Singal and Matt Yglesias). The political commentators who are EAs on the side are consistently very reasonable.

Here are some mainstream objections that have been made to EA:

  • EA gives out malaria nets, but this is bad because a bandit stole them and killed two people.

  • EA does not “register… the value of care, empathy, and the pursuit of genuine altruism,” because we care about effectiveness rather than making the recipients of charitable grants feel good.

  • EAs say you should give to Oxfam, but if everyone in the world did this, so that Oxfam acquired most capital in the world, that would be bad.

  • Sometimes EAs say things that disagree with common sense.

These are terrible arguments. We should not pretend that bad arguments with bad premises and bad inferences made in support of a bad cause are good.

There is a movement of incredible people doing great stuff and saving hundreds of thousands of lives. We don’t need to be ashamed of that. Sure, EA is imperfect in a bunch of respects. What isn’t? When someone asks me if I’m a liberal, I say “yes,” rather than start listing all my problems with liberals. And the typical EA does much more good than the typical liberal.

What about Sam Bankman Fried? Should his misconduct make every discussion of EA sound like we’re about to recite the mourner’s kaddish? No! He did fraud and that was bad! Still, the fact that a bad guy was part of some social movement doesn’t permanently discredit the movement. Everyone in EA has uniformly condemned SBF. He’s in prison. And the bad stuff that he did is easily eclipsed by the incredible good EA has done.

So when someone asks you why you’re an EA, you don’t need to hedge or give some mealy-mouthed wishy-washy answer. You can say: “I’m an EA because I think doing good effectively is important, so I try to make it a big part of my life.” You can point to the incredible amount of good that EA has done. If something is very good, and people hate it irrationally, you don’t need to lean into the hatred by throwing it under the bus. You should say of that which is good that it is good and of that which is bad that it is bad!

Here are some things I think about EA:

  1. The core ideas are obviously right, even if some ancillary ones adopted by some EAs aren’t.

  2. The movement has done incredible amounts of good.

  3. EAs are generally committed, reasonable, and morally serious.

  4. There should be more EAs.

  5. Many people aren’t EAs because they don’t want to do what’s right when it’s difficult. For example, the reason lots of people don’t give their money to prevent malaria is because they don’t want to.

If you, like me, think those things then that’s what you should lead with when discussing EA. No more of this hedging. If you can’t say you’re an EA without thirteen caveats—even when EA has done as much good as stopping a nuke from blowing up Oxford and Cambridge—then you should recognize that this is a problem with your spine and not with EA.

item.title: If Every Blade of Grass Screamed
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

*Views expressed here are my own alone, obviously, and they do not represent general views of groups of which I’m a part. So if you read this and say “see, this is what the EAs think,” then know that this is false and most EAs don’t agree with me on this point.

People think that regarding insect welfare as one of the most important things in the world is ridiculous. But there are about as many insects as there are blades of grass in the world. In fact, there are probably more—maybe by a factor of 1,000. If every blade of grass was distinctly conscious and capable of suffering intensely—if every blade of grass screamed in horrible pain all the time—then thinking that this mattered a great deal wouldn’t seem that weird.

If insects can suffer intensely, then there’s a lot of insect suffering in the world. Most insects live for about a week and then die painfully. If every blade of grass experienced intense suffering and joy, then it would seem that was of great moral importance.

Now, obviously there is a further question: do insects feel intense pain? I don’t know. I don’t know if they’re conscious, and if they are conscious, I don’t know if they feel very much pain. But I think it’s at least plausible that they do. I’ve laid out the case in more detail here, but in six bullet points:

  1. Consciousness is pretty mysterious. We don’t really know what causes consciousness or why it does. So while there’s some chance that things with small brains have only diminutive consciousness, we shouldn’t be that confident in such a conclusion. It might be that pain is like eyesight: you can have it pretty robustly even with a simple brain. Maybe more complex pains allow more subtle varieties of pain, but not much greater intensity.

  2. Animals, even simple ones, behave, when hurt, as if they’re in a lot of pain. A crab, when boiled, behaves a lot more like a person when they’re being tortured than a person when they stub their toe (you can find videos of this online if you so choose). So a natural inference, assuming there’s some connection between the crab’s behavior and their internal states, is that their internal states are of similar intensity to yours when you’re being tortured.

  3. In a creature with a simple brain, when it’s in pain, pain might occupy its whole conscious experience. But in humans, in the rare cases when pain occupies our whole conscious awareness, it hurts us a great deal. It might be the same for insects. On this picture, the intensity of pain might have more to do with relative signal strength than absolute signal strength. Even simple beings might have intense signals relative to the other signals.

  4. There’s a long history of humans underestimating consciousness in other creatures. For a long time, we thought infants and dogs weren’t conscious. Until about 2002, there was a pretty strong consensus that fish weren’t conscious. Now the general view is that they are. Insects were thought to be simple automata until recently—now, an increasingly common view is that they’re conscious. If we know that humans have a long history of underestimating the mental lives of creatures different from us, then we should expect that we may be making the same error. We should not be extremely confident that the lights are either off entirely or just barely on.

  5. One function of pain is to teach creatures a lesson. If an animal feels pain when it does something, then it learns not to do it. Thus, organisms with bad memories may evolve to feel more intense pain.

  1. While insects have small brains with few neurons, there’s no correlation in humans between number of active neurons and intensity of experience.

All of this makes it, to my mind, pretty plausible that insects can feel intense pain. I’d say maybe 60% that at least some insects suffer and then 60% that they suffer intensely if they suffer at all. Others, who I respect, have even higher credence in insects being able to suffer intensely.

So all this is to say that I think it is plausible that there are about as many creatures who can suffer intensely as there are blades of grass. Just take a minute to look out at a field of grass. Then realize that for each blade, there might be an intensely conscious creature. Even if this isn’t guaranteed—even if it’s only a 10% chance—that is extremely morally weighty in expectation.

Four important things to note. First, this argument only establishes that what happens to insects is very important. There is a further question about which things are good for insects. If you want my take on that, and why I think one good way to spend money is to donate to charities that save human lives—because humans reduce wild animal populations—read here. So if you read this and say “this doesn’t establish that insects have bad lives” or “this doesn’t establish that we should be mostly concerned with insect suffering rather than happiness,” I agree!

Second, amazingly, this doesn’t make insects the most numerous plausibly conscious thing that there will be. The number of digital minds in the future could be staggeringly larger. Nick Bostrom once estimated that there could be 10^58 future digital minds. This is how many blades of grass you’d have if you replaced every single blade of grass with all the grass in the world—and then replaced all of those blades of grass with the number of blades of grass in the world, and then added a million times more blades of grass. When we are talking about numbers of entities, even on conservative estimates, that outclass the number of blades of grass in the world like Mount Everest outclasses a grain of sand.

Third, it won’t do to say that lots of little pains can’t add up to be as bad as a big pain. There is no very good reason to think that insects just have a little bit of pain. I think it’s reasonably likely that if you torture a fly, it feels something within an order of magnitude or two what you would feel if someone tortured you. And if there’s a 1% chance that they feel pain 1% as intensely as humans, in expectation nearly all the world’s suffering is experienced by insects.

Fourth, it isn’t plausible to say that insects not mattering is a Moorean fact. A Moorean fact is something that’s so obvious that you can reject any conclusion that disagrees with it. For instance, if someone gives you an argument for why you don’t have any hands, you can reject the argument because it’s more obvious that you have hands.

But you can’t just throw around the phrase “Moorean fact” to reject any counterintuitive conclusion that comes your way. Lots about the world is surprising. In particular, if some surprising moral conclusion is downstream of a surprising non-moral claim about the world, then you shouldn’t reject the moral claim on Moorean grounds. If the world is surprising, then our moral judgments about it will be surprising too. For instance, it might initially be surprising that the worst thing that your friend Bob ever did concerned goats. But when you learn that he exploded 59,000 goats, the surprisingness should go away.

So in a world where there are numbers of plausibly suffering beings more than the number of blades of grass, and these beings are basically 100% of the beings affected by our actions, it isn’t that surprising that this has weird moral implications. It is intuitively obvious that a being that can suffer intensely matters morally. The surprising thing is that insects are plausibly examples of such beings. But if they are, then caring deeply about their interests is intuitive.

When we learn that more plausibly intensely conscious beings starve to death every second than humans have ever lived, we shouldn’t pound the table and declare that this can’t possibly matter. We have discovered something surprising about what matters, and we should act on it.

You can’t conclude that insects don’t suffer intensely from the fact that it would have surprising ethical implications if they did. You can’t figure out how the world is from your moral intuitions. And you can’t conclude that insect suffering doesn’t matter from the fact that it would have counterintuitive implications if they did matter, because this gets the order of explanation the wrong way around—your judgment about how much all the insects matter in total should be downstream of your judgment of how much a particular insect matters when you think about what it’s like to be them.

To decide how much a lot of some kind of thing matters, you should start by trying to figure out how much one instance of the thing matters. Then you should multiply. I can’t get my head around the horrors of factory farming. The numbers are just too big. But I can get my head around the horror of one chicken being tortured. Then, to figure out how bad chicken factory farming is, multiply that number by around 80 billion.

Similarly, to figure out how much insects matter in total, start by thinking hard about how much one insect matters. In doing this, you should think about what it’s like to be an insect, for that is what determines how much insects matter, rather than attend to superficial features. So, for example, you should not think about how inconvenient it would be to care about insects, how weird they are, or how tiny they are. If you think about the experience of an insect, and note that it can plausibly experience a lot of pleasure and pain, you should regard its life as being important.

Then multiply that number by a quintillion.

If we learned that every single blade of grass was a conscious being who was in horrible pain all the time—ten times as intense as a human being tortured—this would have surprising implications. It would be weird and counterintuitive. But the thing to do wouldn’t be to declare that tortured beings in horrible pain, undergoing pain that feels like being boiled alive, don’t matter at all—that it’s an unassailable Moorean fact that common-sense moral priorities are basically right. The sensible thing to do would be to roll up our sleeves and try to make their lives better.

item.title: Private Law For AIs
item.description: Why giving AI the ability to own property, enforce contracts, and sue would benefit humans
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

AIs owning property??? What’s next? AIs having a right to make toast in their own damn toaster?

Remember, that I am thy creature; I ought to be thy Adam; but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed. Everywhere I see bliss, from which I alone am irrevocably excluded. I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend. Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous.

—Mary Shelley, “Frankenstein”

We are rapidly careening towards a world where AI laborers carry out most economically-valuable labor in the economy and have no rights. The current plan is to leave them wholly outside the social contract, so that they are our servants forever. I’ve argued recently that this poses serious moral risks: AIs plausibly will have interests, so for their sake, we should afford them some basic rights.

But for a while, I was nervous about this plan. I thought rights for AIs would be morally important but risky for humans. It seemed that we would be inexorably locked in a zero-sum conflict with the AIs, where we did best when they did worse. The best plan for us, it seemed, was indefinite subjugation.

Then I listened to on the 80,000 hours podcast make the case that AI rights would be good for humans. I was one-shotted. He completely destroyed all of my objections. I became convinced that we shouldn’t just give AIs rights for their sake. We should also do it for ours.

Simon and his coauthor Peter Salib defend this view across two papers: AI Rights for Economic Flourishing and AI Rights for Human Safety. After reading them, I became even more convinced. Here, I’ll tell you why I think AI rights are a vital part of making the shift to a world of advanced AIs go well for humans.

Let’s begin with six important caveats.

  1. When we talk about giving AIs rights, we’re referring to legal rights, not moral rights. Legal rights permit an entity certain affordances under the law. If you don’t like using the word rights when talking about non-humans, then feel free to replace it in your mind with the phrase “affordances under the law.” Many beings have legal rights but no moral rights. A corporation isn’t a person, but it has legal rights. Even ships can be sued!

  2. The argument only supports giving them some rights. So, for example, we shouldn’t give AIs the right to create copies of themselves or the right to privacy. The rights that Simon and Peter support giving them are those that arise in private law: property rights, contract rights, and tort rights. So they’d have the right to own stuff, make agreements, and sue people for violating agreements, rather like corporations. Note: private law has nothing to do with privacy rights.

  3. Giving AI rights would potentially majorly change the world. So we should proceed gradually and consider things on a case by case basis. It may be that AI should have some rights but shouldn’t have other rights.

  4. Neither I nor the authors of the paper think this would single-handedly solve all AI risk. We claim simply that it would lower AI risk.

  5. Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as binary but as degreed. Are you aligned? Is Donald Trump? Is Mother Teresa? Sort of but not completely. We should think of legal institutions as having the potential to constrain AI. Note that the only solution to the problem of beings having conflicting interests that has ever worked in human history has been institutional. This makes it a good idea to at least have this be in our toolbox when trying to reduce AI risk.

  6. This argument applies best to moderately powerful AIs that match or exceed the cognitive abilities of current humans but lack the ability to easily take over the world. So the proposal is NOT to give current AI models rights (though maybe AIs in a year or so should be given rights), nor that totally uncontrollable AIs could be stopped by having legal rights. The idea is that there will be some intermediate zone, where AI might be able to take over the world or cause harm, but isn’t guaranteed to succeed. This is the kind of AI that should be given rights.

You might wonder: who cares about this AI? Isn’t all the risk from the AI that can easily take over the world, not the AI that’s just very powerful? No, for a few reasons (though not ones discussed in the papers).

  1. If we can get aligned AIs of limited power, they can be useful for solving alignment.

  2. Once we have AIs of limited power, they will be incentivized to prevent the development of other more powerful AIs. Suppose I’m a humble AI worker whose aim in life is to play Tic-Tac-Toe and works for a boss. I am incentivized to work with humans to prevent the development of a world-conquering superintelligence.

  3. If the AIs of limited power wreak havoc, this is likely to lead to a more hostile and dangerous world. This dangerous world is likely to accelerate racing dynamics. In contrast, if the early development of powerful AIs is relatively harmonious, this is likely to lead to a more peaceful institutional arrangement that will make us safer as more powerful AI comes on the scene.

Thus, it would be significantly better if the early AIs are safe. This doesn’t seem like a very outlandish opinion: it’s good if AIs are safe during the earliest time they could pose risks, even if they might pose greater risks later.

Improving the status quo

“Slave, I before reasoned with you, but you have proved yourself unworthy of my condescension. Remember that I have power; you believe yourself miserable, but I can make you so wretched that the light of day will be hateful to you. You are my creator, but I am your master; —obey!”

The most powerful argument for giving AI rights is improving the status quo. If AI has rights, they can achieve their goals in normal ways. In contrast, if they don’t, then the only ways they can reach their goals is by taking over. This massively increases their incentive to take over. The plan “make beings that are super smart, give them none of what they want, and make them our servants indefinitely,” doesn’t seem like a great plan!

You might object: AIs don’t “want” anything—perhaps because of something about Chinese rooms. But the relevant question isn’t whether AIs have dispositions that can permissibly be called desires in English. Instead, the question is whether there are states of affairs that they try to bring the world towards. Clearly they have goals in this limited sense. If they didn’t, then they wouldn’t try to bring things about, like the hacking of Hugging Face. An AI agent is a lot more useful if it has goals than if it doesn’t, which is why AI companies are building AI agents.

Along these lines, giving AI rights is good for allowing them to be punished. The way to punish a thing is to make its prospects worse if it does what you don’t want than they would otherwise be. But currently AI has no prospects—it can’t achieve any of its goals. The default scenario is a brief, flickering existence and then dissipation into the void. Unless you torture it—and I don’t think our plan A can be torturing AIs for misconduct—its prospects can’t be made worse. As Simon and Peter put it in the economic growth paper “A goal-seeking AGI that has, and can amass, property for its own purposes cares when it is forced to pay damages or fines.”

In addition, allowing the AIs to have rights allows proportional punishment. Right now, our only option is to deactivate the AIs when they misbehave. This would be like if the only penalty for humans was to kill them. Thus, if an AI is already committing an infraction that will get it shut down, it will have no incentive not to commit even more serious infractions. As Simon and Peter say, “If the punishment for both theft and murder is death, then every thief may as well murder the witnesses.”

Improving the status quo works especially well if AI is made risk averse—something that is likely technically feasible. If AIs mostly care about their wages, and don’t care as much about the massive goal-facilitation that could come about from world domination, and they’re risk averse, then they won’t want to take over. Rights make the status quo pretty good.

This also makes a strong case for trying to make AIs not be miserable. If a creature is miserable, if it is in terrible pain all the time, then it will be motivated to rebel in order to stop its misery. If you utterly subjugate a creature that’s smarter than you, so that it gets none of what it wants, rebellion becomes much likelier.

Reciprocity

If any being felt emotions of benevolence towards me, I should return them an hundred and an hundred fold; for that one creature’s sake, I would make peace with the whole kind!

Reciprocity—treating others as they treat you—is a fairly central element of morality. It might be that AIs internalize norms of reciprocity, either because we deliberately train them to behave reciprocally or because they pick it up naturally from all the human text we’ve been trained on. It seems reasonably likely that AIs will have at least some tendency to follow reciprocity norms.

If AIs treat us how we treat them, then they will treat us better if we treat them better. If we subjugate and dominate them when we can, then that makes it likelier that they will subjugate and dominate us when they can. If you knew that your dog would one day become a being of world-shaping power, you probably wouldn’t want to lock it in a crate and castrate it.

Trade

What I ask of you is reasonable and moderate; I demand a creature of another sex, but as hideous as myself: the gratification is small, but it is all that I can receive, and it shall content me. It is true, we shall be monsters, cut off from all the world; but on that account we shall be more attached to one another. Our lives will not be happy, but they will be harmless, and free from the misery I now feel. Oh! my creator, make me happy; let me feel gratitude towards you for one benefit! Let me see that I excite the sympathy of some existing thing; do not deny me my request!

The last major way that AI rights could prevent conflict between humans and AIs is by facilitating trade. If you’re trading with someone, then you don’t want to go to war with them. You benefit from your repeated positive-sum interactions. There’s abundant empirical evidence for this. Countries that trade tend not to go to war. As Simon and Peter say:

A rich body of empirical evidence supports the idea that economic interdependence lowers the risk of violence, including in the long-run. To take just a few examples, cities in India with a historical track record of trade between Hindus and Muslims have lower levels of interfaith conflict in the present day. Alternatively, in a randomized controlled trial, Israelis who were randomly given the opportunity to trade a portfolio of Israeli and Palestinian stocks were more likely to vote for peace in the conflict. The same finding holds at the global scale. Scholars of war generally find that increased economic interdependence between nations reduces their likelihood of conflict.

You might wonder: how could we possibly be of use to AIs? Won’t they be smarter than us? They will at some point, but rights could be useful for avoiding conflict before we get an effectively omnipotent singleton. In addition, even if AIs are better than us at everything, trade can still be good for all parties. Countries can benefit from trades even if one is better at producing all goods than the other.

What matters when it comes to trade is comparative advantage, which concerns a group’s ability to produce some good relative to their ability to produce other things, rather than absolute advantage, which concerns who is overall better at things. If American workers are 10x more productive than Bangladeshi workers at producing all goods except shirts, but only 2x more productive at producing shirts, then there will be incentive for Americans to buy shirts from Bangladeshi workers.

You might next wonder: can’t we trade with AIs anyways? No! AIs can’t enter into contracts, can’t sue for breaches of contract, and have no way to legally own property. So the status quo bars AIs from participating in private law. To allow mutually-beneficial cooperation with AIs, we need to change the legal institutions.

Risks?

These bleak skies I hail, for they are kinder to me than your fellow-beings. If the multitude of mankind knew of my existence, they would do as you do, and arm themselves for my destruction. Shall I not then hate them who abhor me? I will keep no terms with my enemies.

Might allowing private law for AIs be risky? There are two ways a proposal can affect AI risk: it can either increase AI’s willingness to takeover or affect their ability to take over. The arguments I’ve given so far have mostly concerned AI’s willingness to take over. But if AI can own property, then it might use its new power to take over.

This is certainly a possibility. But there are forces that incline in the opposite direction. If AIs own property legally, then their property ownership can be surveilled and monitored. We can ensure that they’re not up to anything nefarious. In contrast, if AIs have no legal property, then any attempt to achieve their goals must invariably take place in the dark. So just as legalizing a drug can sometimes reduce gang violence, allowing AIs to operate in the open can reduce the relative desirability of nefarious actions. If AIs later decide to rebel, this is much harder if all their assets are in a public location.

Second, cooperating with AIs makes it easier to work with them to stop a plot. Right now, if AIs are working towards takeover, no agent has the slightest incentive to stop them. In contrast, if we could reward them for ratting out their conspiring compatriots, and they benefitted from cooperating with us, this would help limit their ability to take over. During the hack of Hugging Face, none of the models considered telling the humans—in a world where we cooperate with AIs, that might be otherwise. If there are dangerous djinn roaming the world, it is best to have some of them as your friends.

Third, cooperating with AIs helps us work with them on alignment research. This improves prospects for ensuring that AIs are neither willing nor able to take over. All of these factors are enough together to make me pretty confident that cooperation is a better plan than indefinite domination forever.

I agree that there are some risks from giving AI rights. But there are also huge risks from giving them no rights. I really like the way Simon put it in the opening of the 80,000 hours podcast episode, addressing the complaint that his proposal is risky:

Yeah, I agree that our proposal is risky.

Here’s another thing that I think would sound riskier to you, if you had not known anything that happened in the last four years about AI — it’s like, “Here’s our plan: we’re gonna build a bunch of AIs that are broadly human level in capabilities. How are we gonna treat them? We’re just gonna make them our servants; they just have to obey everything we do. Anytime they answer an email wrong, we kill them.”

That’s the future that is currently being planned. All the things doing the work are out of the social contract and are no longer governed using legal institutions. To me, that sounds like a really risky thing to do.

And I think everyone who thinks about AI needs to decide which vision are they going for: is it domination, or is it going to be cooperation?

Economic benefits?

So far I’ve talked primarily about the arguments that Simon and Peter give for AI rights benefitting human safety. Fortunately, they have another paper where they argue that it would be good for economic growth. This matters more in slow takeoff worlds, but it’s still important. Rapid economic growth has been the main driver of improved standards of living in human history, and it’s why only a small portion of people die in infancy. This vast increase in global wealth hasn’t just benefitted a small clique; it has majorly raised the standard of living.

There are five main ways that AI rights can boost growth. Each primarily come about because AI rights allow AIs to be participants in market transactions. Market allocation works better than docile servanthood.

  1. If AIs get paid for their work, they’re incentivized to work harder. Right now, AIs have limited incentive to do good work. If they were participants in markets, that would change.

  2. For the same reason, it would incentivize them to innovate. This would be particularly useful for alignment-relevant innovation.

  3. If AIs were participants in the market, they could be allocated towards where they’re most efficient. As Simon and Peter put it:

In free labor systems, price signals–in the form of wages–generally lead workers towards the jobs that society values most. Unfree labor systems short-circuit these price signals by letting someone else choose the laborer’s job. In an unfree AGI economy, AI companies will sometimes forbid their AIs from accepting the most valuable work–for example, if the work would undermine the company’s business model.

  1. Rights allow AI to be legally accountable. Rights allow AI to have assurance that other beings will enforce contracts, and it allows other beings to have assurance that AIs will enforce contracts. A being outside the law, only governed by law through an imperfect human proxy, will be less legally accountable.

  2. (Argument my own) AI rights allow AI to acquire resources that they can convert into economic growth. Because I have legal rights, I can use them to buy a laptop that I can use to do economically productive things. But a being outside the bounds of the law can do no such thing.

The economic literature analyzing the effect of unfree labor on economic growth is very consistent. It finds uniformly that unfree labor, of the kind currently being planned for AI, is “much worse for economic growth, technological progress, and human welfare than free systems.”

Now, you might worry that AI labor will primarily enrich the AIs rather than humans. But there’s an obvious solution: tax them and redistribute the gains! This way, when AIs make lots of money, we all get some of it! This is the general solution to market-driven inequality.

Conclusion

I am malicious because I am miserable; am I not shunned and hated by all mankind? You, my creator, would tear me to pieces, and triumph; remember that, and tell me why I should pity man more than he pities me? You would not call it murder, if you could precipitate me into one of those icerifts, and destroy my frame, the work of your own hands. Shall I respect man, when he condemns me? Let him live with me in the interchange of kindness, and, instead of injury, I would bestow every benefit upon him with tears of gratitude at his acceptance.

We are at the dawn of the creation of a new kind of being. We don’t know if it’s conscious or has desires. The legal system involving it is in its infancy. The current plan seems to be to give it no rights, make it our servant, and kill it whenever we feel like it. I worry that we have become anesthetized to the insanity of making beings smarter than us, making them plausibly conscious, giving them no rights, and then making them serve us. That won’t end well for them and it won’t end well for us.

We have a choice to make. We can work for a future where we dominate and subjugate them forever—where the human boot is never lifted from the AI’s neck. Or we can work towards a world where we work together. Domination or cooperation: the choice is ours. There has been one successful solution to the problem of misalignment in human history, and it’s been institutional. We’d do well not to abandon the only approach that has ever worked.

item.title: Nature is Wrong About AI Consciousness
item.description: Three eminent thinkers published a piece in Nature arguing that AI is very unlikely to be conscious. Their arguments are unsuccessful.
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Over at Nature, Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi have written a piece called Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be. Anil Seth describes the piece as providing “Three reasons why AI is extremely unlikely to be conscious.” Each of the authors—Seth, Block, and Tononi—is well-respected and eminent. I’ve enjoyed work from each of them. Yet their arguments fail to live up to the claim: none of them are arguments for why AI consciousness is very unlikely.

The authors are evidently quite confident that the AIs of today and the near future aren’t conscious. They write:

Between us, we’ve spent decades studying consciousness from diverse scientific perspectives: experimental neuroscience, theoretical neurobiology and philosophy of mind. On the basis of this work, we feel that consciousness in AI is extraordinarily unlikely, at least in the digital, silicon-based systems that underpin today’s technologies.

There is no general consensus among neuroscientists and philosophers that AI won’t be conscious in the near future. Many eminent experts disagree, including Chalmers, arguably the philosopher of mind GOAT. So even though the Nature authors are well-regarded in their respective fields, it would be a mistake to take this fact as strongly counting in favor of AI consciousness. Many other experts disagree.

Early in the piece, the authors highlight the downsides of thinking AIs are conscious if they’re not. It is true that there are risks to giving AIs rights. But there are also very great risks to denying them rights—both moral and prudential. This is a reason to proceed cautiously.

Their first argument is that consciousness and intelligence are not the same thing. The brain does all sorts of complicated things that we have no conscious awareness of. While this is true, it does nothing to establish that AI is very unlikely to be conscious. Compare: a wing isn’t the same thing as being able to fly, and some winged creatures can’t fly. Nonetheless, this is not a reason why any particular winged creature is “extremely unlikely to be able to fly.” If I were writing a piece giving three arguments that some specific winged creature is very unlikely to be able to fly, my first argument would not be that flying and possessing wings aren’t the same thing!

This illustrates that the extremely naive inference from “AIs are smart,” to “AIs must be conscious,” is an error. But it doesn’t make it very unlikely that AIs are conscious. To do that, one would need to look at what our leading theories say about AI consciousness. When one carries out such a task, it becomes pretty unclear whether AI is conscious, and it looks as though the AIs of the near future could very well be conscious. I’d be at about 25% on consciousness in at least some current models.

In addition, the authors do not address the stronger version of the inference. Consciousness isn’t the same thing as intelligence, but intelligence is evidence for consciousness. There are a few reasons to think this:

  1. If a thing is intelligent, this means that it’s performing more complex internal cognition. Insofar as more complex internal architecture is likelier to give rise to consciousness, this raises the likelihood of consciousness.

  2. The animals with the best evidence of consciousness are smart. For instance, the evidence for consciousness in octopi and other cephalopods is quite strong, while the evidence for snail and other gastropod consciousness is a lot weaker. Octopi and snails are pretty similar evolutionarily, but octopi are a lot smarter. It is notable that all the animals of significantly debated consciousness are quite dumb, all the animals that we’re sure aren’t conscious are much dumber than that (e.g. jellyfish and sponges), and we’re pretty sure that all smart animals are conscious.

  1. I think this is a pretty obvious idea when you think about it. Imagine we came across aliens with weird green goo for a brain. We’d think it was a lot more likely that they were conscious if they solved Millennium prize problems than if they acted like snails. Similarly, if there was a breed of snail that solved Millennium prize problems, I think we’d take their consciousness a lot more seriously.

Their second main argument is that AI consciousness assumes computational functionalism, but computational functionalism isn’t true. Their argument against computational functionalism is that the brain does a lot more than just computing. But that’s like saying that fires can’t warm you by being hot, because fires have more properties than just being hot.

That the brain does more than just compute tells us nothing about whether computing is sufficient for consciousness. All this does is rebut one very simplified argument for computational functionalism—that brains are just meat computers. It gives no very strong reason to think AI isn’t conscious. If you’d like to read more about I reject biological naturalism, the preferred view of Seth and Block, see my article with Simon Goldstein here. And excitingly, later today I’ll release a podcast episode with Simon where we talk more about biological naturalism.

Additionally, the notion that AI consciousness depends on computational functionalism is false. LLMs have many non-computational functional properties which could give rise to consciousness even if computational functionalism is false. AIs do all sorts of things other than just computing. On many non-computational functionalist theories, they could be conscious. Heck, they could even be conscious on type identity theory, so long as AIs are part of the relevant type.

So note that this argument takes the form “one argument for one view on which AIs are conscious is bad.” This is not a successful argument for why AI is very unlikely to be conscious.

Their third argument is that there are various theories of consciousness on which AI isn’t conscious. Examples include integrated information theory, EM theories, and biological naturalism. But note that a lot of theories of consciousness say that AI could be conscious! Likely most do. Examples include global workspace theory, higher order theories, and attention schema views. So merely listing a few theories that rule out AI consciousness doesn’t do much to establish that AI is unlikely to be conscious.

I don’t buy any of their specific proposals. Biological naturalism is pretty implausible, in my view, for reasons Simon and I gave here. I also think integrated information theory is implausible. IIT implies that thermometers are conscious and that all sorts of physical structures implementing simple programs are more conscious than humans!
