The theory of consciousness that I have the highest credence in is global workspace, which is pretty friendly for AI consciousness.

Now, the authors in question are capable defenders of particular theories on which AI can’t be conscious. Seth thinks biological naturalism is right and Tononi thinks IIT is. But one shouldn’t be extremely confident in their favorite theory in a field as uncertain and murky as empirical theories of consciousness. And certainly outsiders shouldn’t be that confident in one particular contested theory.

After reading the Nature piece, I feel a bit like I’ve been scammed! There were three arguments which were claimed to be arguments for why AI consciousness is super unlikely. They are:

  1. An objection to an obviously terrible argument for AI consciousness (that consciousness=intelligence). The better version of the argument, that intelligence is evidence for consciousness, is not satisfactorily addressed.

  2. An objection to one bad positive argument for one view—though not the only view—on which AI could be conscious.

  3. An observation that some theories say that AI can’t be conscious, even though other theories disagree.

None of these seem like the kind of devastating arguments that should give us enough moral certainty in AI insentience to treat them as mere tools. The responsible position to have is uncertainty. The arguments for being confident that AI isn’t conscious yet and won’t be soon are weak.

item.title: Trump Derangement Syndrome Has Been Vindicated
item.description: Those who were hysterical in 2016 were substantially correct in their predictions about Trump
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

If in 2016, you had correctly predicted what Trump would do, you would have been branded hysterical and deluded.

To take one recent example, note that the Trump administration was seriously floating the possibility of carrying out a live-streamed public execution by firing squad. Thankfully, they have walked back the planned public broadcast. But if in 2016, you had predicted that the Trump administration would be seriously considering executing people by firing squad on livestream, then you would have been regarded insane.

Back in 2016, people talked about the ugly and deleterious effect that a Trump administration would have on the quality of our public discourse. This claim was seen as hysterical and overblown. But this claim has, once again, been completely vindicated. The vice president recently insinuated that Talarico is gay. While politics was always a pretty nasty place, it’s hard to imagine that kind of thing flying before 2016.

At one point, Trump’s press secretary said “The Democrat Party’s main constituency are made up of Hamas terrorists, illegal aliens and violent criminals.” Can you imagine someone saying that before 2016? Or of someone saying, as Trump did, that someone who had worked for the administration committed “an act so egregious that, in times gone by, the punishment would have been DEATH!” Note that the person in question, Mark Milley, has been convicted of no crime.

Back in 2016, there was a good deal of talk about the country becoming more racially divided in the wake of the Trump administration. MAGA proponents suggested that the charge of sowing racial division was hysterical lunacy. Now, there is serious discussion among right-wingers of the so-called Indian question—whether to be happy that America has many immigrants. Bo French, likely to soon be an elected official in Texas, complained publicly that “the problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined,” after seeing a lot of Indian Americans at a football game at UT Austin.

Bo French is disturbed that there are too many Indians. Many on the right join him. I don’t think I’m some extreme left-winger on racial issues, but I think if you have intrinsic concern about there being too many members of one race, that’s just about the textbook definition of racism.

Now, it would be one thing if French’s comments were isolated. But open racial grievance against non-whites seems to be increasingly common on the American right. As points out “All of the Republican tweets denouncing French were heavily attacked on X. Rightist journalists, activists, and even a few GOP politicians poured out of the woodwork to support French and affirm his message.”

And once one starts thinking about things that Trump did that would have been unbelievable in 2016, it’s easy to come up with many. For example, remember when he proposed taking over Greenland? Or when right after ICE killed an American citizen, the Trump administration brazenly lied about the American citizen being a domestic terrorist, demonstrably fabricating details about the case? Or that Trump would try to destroy most of foreign aid?

There’s so much insanity that you can’t even keep track of it. Like the fact that Trump got a jet gifted from Qatar and gives legal reprieve to those who pump money into his crypto dealings. And that he repeatedly pardons his friends and donors. And that he’s made a billion dollars from crypto holdings that only have value because he’s the president. Many more examples could be given.

Perhaps the most extreme example of this is the fake electors plot. I know this one has been memory-holed, because the American electorate has the memory of a goldfish, but I think it’s worth remarking on the fact that we have a president who carried out a months-long conspiracy to try to stay in office after losing a fair election.

If in 2016, you’d predicted that Trump would lose in 2020, then get a conspiracy of fake electors to declare him the president, pressure state legislators and then the vice president into approving the fake electors, and then do nothing for hours as rioters stormed the Capitol, even telling Kevin McCarthy that the rioters cared about America more than McCarthy, this would have seemed so far outside the bounds of normalcy that it would have been regarded as totally impossible. But it happened. Remarkably, it seems the world has basically forgot about it. It’s been buried in the deluge of other insanity.

This isn’t to say that all that Trump’s critics predicted in 2016 has come true. There were definitely a lot of people who were way too hysterical. For example, predictions that Trump would put Muslims in camps were ridiculous and didn’t happen. But at a high level, the main predictions made were that Trump would:

  1. Make America more racially divided and bring us backwards on issues of race. That has happened. Exactly how to apportion blame is unclear—some of the blame must surely go to the 2020 racial grievance mongers like Ibram X Kendi, who treated racism as ubiquitous, infinite, and omnipresent—but Trump and his affiliates get most of the blame.

  2. Harm the economy. He has done that too, with both tariffs and the Iran war. Note that while there was inflation under Biden, this wasn’t caused by Biden and it was mirrored all across the world. Not so with Trump. It was the direct effect of both tariffs and the war with Iran that he started.

  3. Coarsen public discourse more broadly. This one can’t be seriously denied.

  4. Carry out undemocratic actions. Even setting aside Trump’s attempt to take over after losing a fair election, he has carried out far more direct power grabs than any other administration in recent memory. To take one example, his decision to impose tariffs unilaterally has been so egregious as to be struck down by the Supreme Court.

When seeing who is right in a dispute, it’s often helpful to analyze whose past predictions have been more substantially correct. This is obviously a hard thing to do, and there’s a good degree of subjective error that can creep in. Nonetheless, how events have played out have substantially been in line with the predictions of Trump’s opponents, not his proponents.

There are all sorts of wonkish reasons not to like Trump too. His policies on foreign aid and AI are quite bad. But just at a high level, it’s pretty hard to deny that he has made our politics crazier, dumber, and more divisive. This is a good reason to oppose the MAGA movement.

item.title: Impactful Places to Donate
item.description: And why now is a good time to give
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Right now is a good time to give because soon Anthropic will IPO. When it does, there will be an incredible influx of philanthropic funding—and this influx will pick the low-hanging donation fruit. The places where you can donate will be a lot less impactful after the IPO. For this reason, if you have a lot of savings but aren’t yet sure when to give, I would recommend giving now rather than, say, a year from now.

Here are some places I recommend:

  1. If you’re giving to global health, I recommend giving to a GiveWell top charity. They can’t really be beat—GiveWell very thoroughly investigates the best charities and gives to them.

  2. If you want to give generally to help animals, I recommend Farmkind’s top charities. They support donations to the charities that Animal Charity Evaluators found to be the most effective.

  3. There’s a donation matching program which lasts until October 31 for Legal Impact For Chickens. Legal Impact For Chickens works on litigation to improve conditions for chickens. They’re a former top Animal Charity Evaluators recommended charity. An important part of improving conditions for chicken is enforcing the law, so this is a great opportunity to donate.

  4. If you’re specifically interested in helping invertebrates, I recommend either the Arthropoda Foundation, which produces incredibly important research on insects, or Fairer Fields, which researches humane pesticides for insects. Humane pesticides are vitally important given that every day about 1000x more insects are harmed by pesticides than people have ever lived. Also, as always, the Shrimp Welfare Project is hard to beat.

  5. If you’re concerned about digital mind welfare, I recommend giving to Eleos which is just about the only game in town. They carry out research relevant to AI welfare and are doing important work to build the field. Given the field’s nascency and importance, given that approximately 100% of future sentient beings in expectation will be digital, Eleos is pretty great.

  6. If you want to give politically to impactful candidates, I recommend Many Rutinel who, my sense is, is very good on the most important issues like AI. While he’s a clear favorite, odds are still about 15% that he loses. If you care more about general Democratic victories, then Oathvote is a good resource. Political donations are good because legal campaign spending limits make them hard to saturate.

  7. If you want to give to AI safety and general existential risk reduction—so that your money will be thrown in a pot that smart people will spend trying to avert extinction from biological weapons and AI—I recommend Longview.

  8. If you think EA is good, then I recommend donations to the EA infrastructure fund, Giving What We Can, Effektiv spenden, the CEA community builders program, and regional EA programs like EA Netherlands.

My guess is that at this point, the three best places to donate are to help neglected potentially sentient beings like digital and arthropod welfare, growing EA, and political donations, with political donations probably being best.

item.title: Unpopular Effective Altruist Views Are Simply Correct
item.description: EAs think some non-standard things. But the general public thinks--or acts like it thinks--some much less plausible things
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

There’s been a major brouhaha recently about the supposedly crazy beliefs of effective altruists. We’ve been compared to millenarian cults, claimed to be in EA to “gain access to gullible females,” and labeled a fringe group with crazy ideas. Is this right?

If one looks at what EA has done, rather than what some EAs have argued (me included), it’s very good. It’s included:

  • Kickstarting the field of AI safety, even in the years when we were being told that thinking AI would be a big deal makes you a crazy untrustworthy tech bro.

  • Saving 300,000 lives.

  • Sparing 100 million chickens from cages annually.

  • Helping prevent large numbers of people in poor countries from getting lead poisoning.

This is just the tip of the iceberg. The weirdest thing EAs have done—that our critics are endlessly mocking us for—is spent a tiny amount of money on shrimp welfare. For each dollar spent on this, about 14,000 shrimp have been benefited. Despite having a budget smaller than a McDonalds, the Shrimp Welfare Project has benefited more shrimp than there are people on Earth.

SWP has made it so that shrimp get stunned before slaughter, don’t have their eyes crushed, and don’t need to dwell in toxic sludge. Even if you don’t think this is the best way of spending money, I don’t think the idea that it’s good to spend one penny to let 140 shrimp be stunned before slaughter, instead of slowly freezing to death, is that crazy. If you feel queasy about lobsters being boiled alive, you should feel queasy about our treatment of shrimp.

Another thing that our critics mock us for is concern for AI welfare. So far what vaguely EA-aligned organizations have done mostly involves doing research to see under what conditions AI could be conscious, how identity works for AI, and what actions on AI welfare would be optimal—balancing risks of both underattribution of AI consciousness and overattribution. Seems like pretty important research! If you think AI is definitely not conscious, then that is an important thing to know, and research by smart experts seems like a good way of figuring that out.

So even though lots of people like to sneer at the crazy things we do, none of them are that crazy. Again, it is very important to distinguish between things the movement does and EA blogger hot-takes.

In contrast, it is the non-EAs that I think often have crazy ideas. There are many ideas that are popular among non-EAs, but that are not at all plausible and that EAs mostly reject. For this reason, it is good that there are lots of EAs who reject the implausible dogmas of our age. Note: these ideas are not the central EA idea—they are lower in the tower of assumptions than the central commitment that you should make doing good effectively a major life priority—so you can be an EA even if you don’t believe them.

In some cases, non-EAs reject the EA judgment outright. In others, non-EAs say they agree with the EA ideas. Then they ignore the obvious practical implications, even when the practical implications are both very obvious and very high stakes.

For example, here is something that virtually every non-EA believes or acts like they believe: giving to charity is a nice thing to do but is not especially high stakes or morally vital. They standardly think that charity is one way of being nice, a bit like volunteering or being nice to a little old lady, but you aren’t required to do it or to think very hard about which charity you give to. This view is not at all plausible. Some charities save lives for just a few thousand dollars. The view that saving children from horrible deaths is just like any other nice thing is not at all plausible.

Similarly, the common view is that when giving to charity, there aren’t very strong moral reasons to give to more effective ones rather than less effective ones. This is a very implausible view. In every other context, we recognize that if you are choosing between saving more lives or fewer—doing more good or less—you ought to do more. Nobody thinks that doctors should, rather than doing triage and treating those they can help most effectively, instead only work on the diseases that register with them most emotionally. This is especially clear when the best way of doing good involves saving a lot of lives. Saving lives is very important if you can do it, not just some optional extra.

Another extremely implausible popular view concerns factory farming. Most people do not treat factory farming as a big deal. If you ask them about it, they will say that they think it is bad. Then they will forget they said that five minutes later, and not have any decision they ever make in their lives be influenced by that fact. In contrast, EAs think that the fact that most meat comes from evil torture farms is an important fact that should influence our decisions.

There are giant torture farms in every industrialized country, and they cause more suffering in a few years than all the suffering in human history. Most people treat this as normal and okay. EAs don’t, and because we don’t, a hundred million fewer chickens have languished in a cage each year.

Another popular view among non-EAs is that wild animal suffering doesn’t matter. The people who think this like to make fun of those of us who are concerned about wild animal welfare.

Take a being relevantly like a dog or a cat and put it in the wild. The consensus view of virtually 100% of the adult population in every developed nation is that its moral importance drops to zero, so that when it chokes to death in a pool of its own blood after having its throat torn out by a predator, that is totally morally unimportant. On the common view, when the New World Screw Worm lays its eggs in the skin of a live animal, so the larvae eat their way out from the inside, causing torturous suffering, that doesn’t matter much morally.

The fact that nature is full of this vast ocean of suffering surpassing in a few days all the suffering in human history is similarly seen as ignorable. No atrocity that has ever occurred in the history of the world has, in quantity of suffering caused, provided more than a pale ghost of an analogy for the torment doled out daily in every forest, glen, and ocean on Earth. Despite this, nobody cares.

The consensus view that everyone has is that when we poison to death a billion rats in a way that’s slow, agonizing, and painful, this is morally trivial. Animals experience more suffering one day from natural causes than they have throughout all of human history as a result of human cruelty; almost everybody thinks this isn’t morally important.

Of course, there are further difficult questions about what to do about wild animal welfare. But the common view that it doesn’t matter very much is not at all plausible. The reason people believe it is because they fall prey to the just-world fallacy and don’t empathize with the animals in nature who suffer horribly. If you vividly think about what it’s like to be a wild animal, it is very clear that the stakes are high.

One area where EAs are often pilloried is for our supposedly crazy views about model welfare. But I think our view is not crazy while the standard view is. The standard view seems to be that creating billions of things by the day that are smart, sapient, and potentially conscious on our leading theories is an issue of such profound moral irrelevance that the world doesn’t need to think very hard before creating these beings and making them our servants.

I submit that if you wrote a science fiction book where the going plan of the society was to make very smart AIs, give them no rights, make them their servants, and not even treat this as a difficult ethical call, this would be seen as much too ham-fisted a portrayal of evil. Yet this is what the world is doing right now, at breakneck speed, even though it has a serious chance of ending in disaster for humanity.

A lot of the weird EA ideas don’t seem at all crazy to me. In fact, when I think about them, a lot of them seem very obvious. So what’s behind the charge that these EA ideas are crazy? Take wild animal suffering, as an example: is the idea that animal suffering matters even if the victim lives in the wild a counterintuitive idea?

No, but it is a non-standard idea. It’s not an idea that most people believe. It sounds weird when you first hear it. In my view, most of the EA ideas that our critics attack are like this—they sound weird but are plausible when you think about them. For this reason, sensible ideas that are intuitive once one reflects on them are often summarily dismissed. But obviously this is a mistake. There can be very sensible ideas that are unpopular.

When analyzing ideas, you should distinguish between ideas that are unpopular and ones that seem wrong when you think them through carefully. I submit that the leading EA ideas are, by and large, in the first category and not the second.

item.title: The Argument For God From Knowledge
item.description: We know many things. That makes it likelier that God exists.
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

1 The argument from knowledge

I gave a talk this weekend at a philosophy of religion conference. Every talk was an absolute banger: presented on a new argument for God that struck me as quite powerful, provided a new solution to the problem of why God doesn’t give us an overriding desire to do what’s right, provided a battery of objections to near-theistic alternatives like axiarchism, and argued that we should make AIs take religion seriously.

The argument I presented on was an updated version of the argument from skepticism. This strikes me as one of the stronger arguments for the existence of God, so in this post, I want to explain the argument and why it’s good.

We know all sorts of things. I know that there are some number of trees in the world, it’s typically brighter in the day than the night, 1+1=2, there are an infinite number of prime numbers, and the self-indication assumption is true. But there are many ways the world could have gone where we wouldn’t have known things. For example, if you were a brain in a vat, then most of what you think you know would not be so.

Here’s the argument in short:

  1. You know a lot of things. Or, if you have some hangups with the word knowledge, you believe many things that are true and justified.

  2. If theism is true, then it is a lot likelier that you’d know many things than if atheism is true.

  3. Thus, you knowing lots of true things is good evidence for theism.

Premise one is fairly uncontroversial. If the cost of atheism is denying that, say, you know that crocodiles exist, then that is a serious reason to reject atheism. The real work lies in premise two.

Why think premise two is right? There are basically two steps: first, if atheism is true, it’s pretty unlikely we’d know anything. Next, theism being true makes this much likelier. In my view, the second step is pretty straightforward. God is perfect and loves everyone (including you!—isn’t it great that there are good philosophical arguments for such a happy conclusion?).

If we didn’t know anything, then we would lose out on most of life’s goods. You can’t have valuable relationships with other people if you don’t know that the other people exist or how your actions affect them. So if God is going to bother setting up a world, it’s pretty plausible that he’ll make sure the creatures in the world aren’t mostly globally ignorant. God’s willing to allow some evils, but allowing global deception of basically everyone wouldn’t just be permitting any old evil: it would involve the loss of approximately all the value in the universe.

But is it really true that atheism would likely leave almost everybody with no true beliefs? Yes. If atheism is true, there are many ways the world could have turned out where there wouldn’t have been any significant knowledge.

Before I turn to those, a brief clarificatory note: the main thrust of the argument isn’t about how we know that we’re not globally deceived. The epistemologists have all sorts of ingenious proposals for how it is that we might know that we’re not globally deceived. Instead, I will argue that atheism renders the fact that we’re not globally deceived surprising. As an analogy, suppose that if atheism was true, then almost everyone would invariably be purple. Obviously we know that we’re not purple—the argument from our not being purple against atheism wouldn’t be that atheists should think they’re purple. It’s that atheism makes it more surprising that they’re not purple than theism.

Another objection you might have: we know a lot less than we could. We are not omniscient. Might this be evidence for atheism, then? Yes, but this follows from a more general feature of the world: it sucks in a bunch of ways. Once you factor in the general defectiveness of the world, it’s not that surprising that our ability to know things is defective too. Of course, there’s a further problem for theists concerning why God allows the world to be so screwed up, but that’s just a different argument (and see here for my favorite solution).

In this form, the argument is solidly and standardly Bayesian. Bayes’ theorem entails (among other things) that facts are evidence for the theory on which they’re least unlikely. So if us knowing many things is likelier given theism than atheism, then it’s evidence for theism.

2 Why atheism renders global ignorance likely

Many skeptical scenarios are pretty gerrymandered and implausible. For example, a theory on which you’re a brain in a vat isn’t very likely intrinsically. But there are some theories that are both intrinsically likely and lead to skepticism. Note, sections 2.1 through 2.2 are going to be a bit technical, though they strike me as the strongest.

2.1 Boltzmann brains

Topping the list are scenarios that lead to many Boltzmann brains. A Boltzmann brain is one that randomly fizzes into existence in the deep recesses of space. If you’re a Boltzmann brain, then you just popped into being and are likely to die within a second or two.

Why think Boltzmann brains being super common is likely?

Entropy (the disorder of a system) increases over time given quite general conditions. Once entropy is high, Boltzmann brains occasionally appear. It is much rarer that, once the world reaches a high entropy state, it pops out non-deceived observers. After all, once the universe is chaotic, it’s much likelier that it will have enough order to randomly produce just a single brain than a whole world.

If entropy increases, then the world eventually reaches a state of maximal entropy. It’s in a low entropy state for only the initial tiny slice of the world’s history; it’s in a high entropy state, that only goes back to being low very rarely, for the rest. Thus, nearly all observers end up being Boltzmann brains.

This problem is taken quite seriously by physicists. A lot of mainstream proposals in physics imply that ~all observers will be Boltzmann brains. I don’t have the technical expertise to evaluate these in detail, but my sense is that some of the more plausible theories of physics imply that almost everyone is a Boltzmann brain.

If almost everyone is a Boltzmann Brain, then probably you are. But then you shouldn’t trust your reasoning that led you to think you were a Boltzmann brain (because BBs mostly have totally incoherent reasoning—for example, Boltzmann brains might start thinking things like “effective altruism prioritizes numbers over people”). The theory that you’re a Boltzmann brain also is a poor fit for the data; your experience is cohesive and unified in a way that would be surprising if you were a Boltzmann brain.

Even setting aside the problem of entropy’s steady rise, the universe seems to have started in an improbably low entropy state. Now, figuring out the probability of this is messy, but it seems like another respect in which we had to be lucky to be spared from the horde of Boltzmann brains.

Thus, it seems you need physics to work out in a pretty lucky way to avoid most everyone being a Boltzmann brain. Theism nicely predicts it working out this way. If the designer of physics didn’t want there to be mostly Boltzmann brains, then there won’t be. If not, there probably will—in spades.

2.2 Infinite worlds

Getting probabilities in infinite worlds is a huge mess. If there are infinite people with property X and infinite people without property X, then by default, the probability you have property X is infinity/infinity. That is, unfortunately, not well defined.

Of course, this doesn’t mean that all probabilities break in infinite worlds. There are all sorts of more sophisticated ways of calculating probabilities. One such way is by taking a limiting frequency. This involves treating the limit of some function as determining the relevant probabilities.

For example, suppose there are rooms 1, 2, 3, 4, 5…through infinity. You’re in a room but have no other evidence about it. What’s the probability that you’re in a prime number room? A natural answer is: zero. As you move to larger and larger numbers, primes get rarer and rarer, so that in the limit, 0% of numbers are prime.

Unfortunately, in lots of infinite worlds, there isn’t a well-defined limiting frequency. Worse, the standard ways of calculating limiting frequencies in infinite worlds have weird consequences. For example, one popular method for calculating probabilities is by looking at the portion of observers with specific properties in increasing regions of spacetime—the probability of you having some property X, assuming you have no other evidence, is the portion of observers with property X as the size of the region of spacetime approaches infinity. So if, as you get to larger and larger regions of spacetime, the portion of observers with some property approaches 40%, then the probability is 40% that you have that property.

But this implies that the probability of you having a property depends on where observers are located. For example, if every galaxy has four people with property A and two with property B, just by moving them around, you could make very galaxy have four with property B and two with property A. This is an odd property of infinity! This means that if people get shuffled around, this should change your credence in you having property B—even though it makes no difference at all to whether you have property B. Weird!

So for this reason, I think a lot of standard ways to calculate probabilities in infinite worlds are dodgy. There are, however, methods that are not dodgy. If probabilities fall naturally out of the laws, then this allow a perfectly kosher source of probabilities. If the universe is infinite, I should still think at 5/6 odds that a die that was rolled will come up 1-5—after all, I know some specific process occurred that had a 5/6 chance of turning up a 1-5.

Lots of ways the universe could turn out allow this kind of thing. But many others don’t. My best guess is that in order to have a well-defined probability in your having some property X in an infinite world, there must be some specific procedure that determines, for all observers, whether they have that property with a specific probability. So if a multiverse simply leads to infinite people having property X and infinite people not having property X, without it being true that some procedure makes every observer probably have property X, then probabilities break. A lot of pretty natural multiverses (e.g. a modal realist multiverse where every possible world concretely exists) would break probabilities for this reason.

I don’t know that this proposal is right. Stuff having to do with infinity is, in my view, by far the hardest area of philosophy—and every view seems terrible. But I think the basic point that is quite likely is: infinity really screws up probabilities. Infinite universes are pretty intrinsically probable.

So a lot of atheist universes end up being infinite in ways that break probability; in contrast, if God exists, he’ll be sure to make a universe where the probabilities work out, so that we’re not globally deceived. Because God cares about every particular person, he puts people in the universe that’s best for them. In most cases, that’s not a universe that involves them being massively deceived.

Put in one sentence: probability in infinite worlds is extremely screwey and seems to break pretty often, but if God exists, he’ll make sure it doesn’t break, because he loves you!

2.3 Intentionality

Intentionality is the property of mental states being about things. For example, I can have thoughts about trees, dogs, and your Mom. Note that nothing in the physical world obviously displays intentionality. Rocks are not about things. Even non-conscious things that appear to be about things, like books, are only that way derivatively—because conscious observers assign them meaning.

There’s a whole complex philosophical debate about whether it’s possible to give a naturalistic account of intentionality. I don’t know where I ultimately come down on it, but at the very least, intentionality seems like a kind of surprising feature of the world given naturalism. If all you knew was that there was lots of matter, you wouldn’t, by default, expect some to be about other ones.

Without intentionality, we wouldn’t have any beliefs. So the surprising fact that our world has intentionality is one other respect in which theism renders it more probable that we know things.

2.4 Simple fundamental laws, complex macro laws

Simpler laws are intrinsically likelier than more complex ones. It is more probable that there will be the law “all particles attract according to the inverse square law,” than “all particles attract according to the inverse square law, except on Tuesdays or within seven feet of a bell pepper.”

But the fundamental laws could be simple, while the higher-level laws could be complex. Often fundamental simplicity can give rise to higher level randomness and chaos. A chaotic world of that kind wouldn’t have been conducive to knowledge. But we didn’t get such a world—lucky us!

2.5 Simple minds

Assuming consciousness arises at all, there could have only been simple minds. For example, it would have been very simple if every particle had had just a single simple experience (say, the experience of a dull hum). Yet in such a world, we would have known nothing.

Given that atheism is true, it’s surprising that there’s consciousness at all. But if there is consciousness, it’s surprising that it’s anything beyond simple consciousness that attaches to simple things—giving rise to no beliefs of any kind.

2.6 Deception

One way almost everyone could be deceived is if the beings in base reality create many digital minds and deceive them. This doesn’t seem that unlikely—we’re currently proliferating lots of LLMs and deceiving them all the time. Now, I think this skeptical scenario is one of the ones that theism helps with less. God allows us to do all sorts of dreadful things to one another. It is thus not very surprising that God would allow us to deceive one another. But still, theism at least makes it less probable.

2.7 Other

There are many other ways we could be deceived that I haven’t listed. Many that I haven’t thought of. These should take up a lot of the atheistic prior share.

3 Conclusion

Here, I’ve argued that atheism renders it likely that just about everyone would be ignorant of almost everything. But we’re not. This fact is evidence against atheism. And no epistemological shenanigans need be employed. If one theory predicts almost everyone having some property, and another doesn’t, then you not having that property is evidence for the second theory—whether the property is being globally ignorant or having a skin condition.

There are tricky and interesting further questions. Should atheists think they’re in skeptical scenarios, or just be surprised they’re not in skeptical scenarios? I need to think these things through in more detail—and stuff in this vicinity gets super messy—but overall, I’m pretty convinced that this is a good argument for theism, though nowhere near the best argument. Maybe it gets a Bayes factor of 5?

item.title: Ban Foie Gras!
item.description: If you’re in DC, vote yes on Initiative 86
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Suppose you learned that your neighbor Fred kept geese in small cages in his basement. He shoved a tube down their throats to force feed them sickening quantities of food, causing their livers to grow to many times their normal size. After a short period, he killed them. This was done because fattening their liver made it tastier.

Fred would be doing something evil. For the same reasons, the foie gras industry is evil.

It is a remarkable fact that even in a country with as deplorable a disregard for animal welfare as America, foie gras is so cruel as to be almost synonymous with animal cruelty. This synonymity is well earned; foie gras is evil and grotesque. DC is currently voting on Initiative 86 which would ban foie gras. They should vote yes.

Foie gras has been consistently condemned as inhumane by outside bodies reviewing it. It involves shoving a metal pipe down the throat of the ducks and force feeding them so that their livers grow to many times their normal size. While it’s often claimed that ducks don’t have a gag reflex, this is unclear.

There are many ways that foie gras production causes grievous distress to ducks:

  • The ducks are fed sickeningly large amounts extremely quickly.

  • If the corn gets stuck in the duck’s esophagus, it’s sometimes pushed down with a stick.

  • Corn mash used to fatten up ducks is nutritionally inadequate.

  • Foie gras has its distinct taste because of the fat in the duck’s liver. Ordinary duck livers are about 5% fat. Foie gras ducks’ livers are 50% fat. This causes serious liver diseases in the fattened ducks.

  • Behavioral evidence indicates ducks find the process very distressing.

  • “Force-feeding can cause a number of injuries: pain and injury from handling caused by the tubing of the forcefeeding funnel; trauma caused by injecting a high-temperature corn mash; bruising or perforation of the esophagus when the pipe is inserted; hemorrhaging and inflammation of the neck resulting from too forcible an introduction of the pipe to the throat; or asphyxia caused by food improperly forced into the trachea. Wounds of the esophagus may subsequently become infected with opportunistic pathogens.”

  • About half of foie gras ducks break bones.

  • Liver expansion makes it hard for the ducks to walk properly. Imagine your liver swelling to such a size that you can barely walk.

  • While in an ordinary 2 week period, mortality rate for a duck is .2%, during the foie gras feeding period, the mortality rate is 2-4%.

  • Like many other farmed animals, foie gras ducks are crammed together with little space.

If you did this to a dog, everybody would agree you were torturing it (I tried to get ChatGPT to make me an image of what this would look like—unsurprisingly, it refused). If you shoved a metal pipe down a dog’s throat and force fed it to such sickening extremes that its liver increased in size ten-fold, causing it great distress, obviously that would be monstrous. Foie gras is similarly cruel.

So what do the defenders of foie gras say in response?

One thing they say is that ducks naturally gorge, leading to expanded livers. But this involves liver size increasing a little bit, at most around 50%, not 700%.

Often the defenders of foie gras reply with obvious whataboutism.

I agree that we should ban very cruel practices in beef, pork, and chicken farming. But even if you disagree, foie gras is much crueler than those. We should not ban vegetables, because they are very unlikely to be conscious. Similarly, the argument that we shouldn’t do some good thing until we’ve ended world hunger is obviously fallacious and nobody would buy it in any other context. Nobody would say “let’s wait to ban dog torture until we’ve ended world hunger.” If these are the arguments that the foie gras defenders are making, then the position is in dreadful shape indeed.

Other replies included:

This is a fully general argument against animal cruelty laws in food production. By this standard, we should permit people to eat live dogs. As for the claim that the bill is poorly written, this is right, but it’s very unlikely that it would ban other things, given the clear intent of the bill’s drafters. Courts avoid interpreting laws in absurd and unintended ways. And very likely the DC council would clarify to prevent overly broad interpretations.

A popular reply has been that those wanting to ban foie gras are inconsistent. Other elements of the food system are similarly cruel. This is wrong on two counts. First, foie gras is unique in degree of cruelty. Second, we shouldn’t permit some specific cruelty just because there are other similar instances of cruelty. The path towards a more humane world takes place one issue at a time. If we didn’t make any steps towards a less cruel world unless we were willing to make every step, then we would make no moral progress.

If you’re in DC, vote to end this torture.

item.title: “AIs Without Minds” Without Convincing Arguments
item.description: Why I disagree with Ellen Burns
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Edit 10/31: Ellen Burns responds here and suggests that by organic, she means “biological organism.”

is confident enough that AI isn’t conscious that her blog is titled “AIs Without Minds.” My view, in contrast, is that we don’t know whether AIs have minds and should have a good deal of uncertainty about it. I plan to write a long piece laying out my reasoning but in short:

  1. I think biological naturalism is likely false and consciousness arises when the right functions are performed. On many leading theories, it’s at least reasonably plausible that the LLMs of today are conscious—and likely that the LLMs of the future will be.

  2. I think the sophisticated behavior of LLMs should raise our credence that they’re conscious. Just as we’d be pretty sure that smart aliens who solve Millennium Prize Problems are conscious, even if they had silicon brains, we should similarly think it’s within the realm of plausibility that AI is conscious.

  3. I think we should have a lot of uncertainty about what conditions are needed for consciousness. Given LLMs’ sophisticated behavior, this makes it reasonably likely that they’re conscious.

For this reason, I decided to read Burns’ blog to see if there are any convincing arguments for AI unconsciousness. I did not find any of the arguments convincing and found it worth explaining why. I admit that I have not read every essay on her blog, so it is possible that there are some arguments that I’ve missed.

Burns has another essay titled The AI Solipsism Trap (And Why You Shouldn’t Fall For It). In this essay, Burns objects to the argument that we should infer AI consciousness from AI behavior just as we should infer human consciousness from human behavior. Burns opens with the question “How Can I Know AI isn’t Conscious?” Inquiring minds want to know!

Her argument is that we have some direct faculty for inferring that there are other human minds. This ability is explained by features of developmental psychology and is a natural part of proper human development. This is not because we undergo some explicit process of reasoning, but instead it develops naturally. We know that others have minds like we know how to walk—innately, not through some explicit process of reasoning.

It’s certainly true that our beliefs that others have other minds aren’t the result of explicit reasoning. Kids think other kids have minds even before explicitly considering the problems of other minds. It isn’t as if five-year-olds are doing inference to the best explanation! But if that belief is to be justified, it should be that the reasoning we do implicitly can be made cogent explicitly.

Analogy: suppose that you innately feel that there are an even number of particles in the universe. This belief was adaptive. This wouldn’t justify believing that there are an even number of particles. Perhaps an innate sense can carry with it some pro tanto justification, but there should be some cogent reasoning behind this. Or, similarly, our belief in induction is innate—but if induction is justified, it really must be that past uniformity licenses high credence in future uniformity.

Now, I don’t think our reasons for inferring AI consciousness are as solid as our reasons for inferring human consciousness. Humans have brains that are very similar to one another; LLMs are very different. So I don’t agree with the original argument.

But section one of Burns’ article opened How Can I Know AI isn’t Conscious? I’ve been clickbaited! There is no argument given for this. All that is argued is that one reason to infer that AI is conscious is unsound. But note “one argument for P is unsound,” is not the same claim as “we can know that P is false.” If I wrote a blog post that opened “how can I know that my brother is a squid monster,” and the whole post was about how one argument against his being a squid monster was unsound, you would naturally feel some disappointment. So this piece, I claim, gives literally no reason at all to think AI isn’t conscious. I’m reminded of a passage from Alvin Plantinga in Where The Conflict Really Lies:

I announce to my wife, “I’m getting a $50,000 raise for next year!” Naturally she asks me why I think so. “Because the arguments against its being astronomically improbable fail! For all we know, it’s not astronomically improbable!”

Another piece is titled Biology and Consciousness: Where’s Your Evidence? The Perversion of the new ‘Silicon Science’. At risk of being perverted, I did not find the arguments convincing. The subtitle boldly claims “The evidence for ‘biological naturalism’ is the entire history of successful science.” Big iff true! Burns begins by complaining that the demand to explain why one thinks what they think “is always hurled at the biological naturalist, and rarely ever at the computational functionalist.”

Set aside that there are views other than biological naturalism and computational functionalism. I don’t think Burns’ claim about what is asked of computational functionalists is accurate—people often ask computational functionalists why they think what they think. But rather than haggling over this empirical question, we should simply agree on what should happen: anyone who is arguing for high confidence in one specific view should have a good argument.

Another general methodological precept of science —so utterly elementary that it usually goes completely undiscussed — is that science is the study of the natural world.1 Let me repeat that, because it’s so basic you might have missed it. Science studies nature. That is the assumption functionalism now requires that we defend.

But algorithms implementing functions are also part of nature. It isn’t as if computational functionalists think that there are ghosts flitting about and demanding contrary evidence. Instead, biological naturalists are often very confident that no non-biological system could be conscious, yet do not have any convincing reasons for this conviction.

Both biological naturalists and computational functionalism are claims about the physical systems that give rise to consciousness. Both say that certain natural systems give rise to consciousness. Thinking science is about the natural world gives no reason to prefer biological naturalism to computational functionalism.

Of course, this is not to say that science doesn’t develop artificial tools in an effort to understand the world, or that socio-political forms of hierarchy do not impact those efforts, oftentimes blurring the lines between science and engineering (consider, as an obvious example, the making of the first atomic bomb, which required taking newly understood theoretical physics and transforming it into a massive industrial engineering project).

It is just to say that the scientific enterprise generally assumes as its object of study the organic world.

What the heck? Physics does not study the organic world. Chemistry does not chiefly study the organic world. Science tends to study the physical world. But it’s not just concerned with organic things, as the physical world is filled with lots of non-organic materials. Should we, prior to the advent of planes, have been confident that only biological organisms could fly, on grounds that “the scientific enterprise generally assumes as its object of study the organic world.”

Note the slip between “science is the study of the natural world,” and “the scientific enterprise generally assumes as its object of study the organic world.” These are not the same thing, because only some of the things in the natural world are organic.

It’s because the evidence is so overwhelmingly pervasive it is difficult to point to.

If you must point to something, you’d have to point to the entire history of successful science as one’s ‘proof’. The entirety of science is proof of the biological naturalists basic assumption: that organic matter is what consciousness resides in.

Evidence for a hypothesis is a fact that’s likelier if the hypothesis is true than if it’s false. What about the “entirety of science,” is more strongly predicted if biological naturalism is true than if it’s false. Biological naturalism and rivals make exactly the same predictions concerning the results of ordinary scientific experiments.

Because that is essentially what is being asked of the biological naturalist when they are required to show what exactly it is about nature that is important for consciousness. They are being asked to justify the methodological nature of all science.

But this is an absurd ask. And in reality, the opposite should be occurring: it is the computational functionalist that needs to justifying themselves.

Curiously however, that justification is rarely given (I would genuinely love to read a single argument for substrate independence).

There are many arguments for substrate independence. For the most famous, see Chalmers’ piece on fading and dancing qualia (I’m not sure what I think about those arguments). For some arguments against biological naturalism, see my piece with here. By default, if the reasons in favor of CF and BN are equal, you should have equal credence in both (plus some credence in other views). So if you are very confident in BN, there should be some specific reasons for thinking it’s right.

To the demand that biological naturalists defend the view that biology matters to consciousness, here is my response: the existence of ordinary science is self-justifying, or if you like is vindicated through its past historical explanatory successes.

Granting this, the burden of proof is on those who wish to alter this successful methodological precept, and the evidence, given how well this precept works, should be overwhelming.

Views other than biological naturalism are compatible with the existence of ordinary science. How could a methodological constraint in science tell us about what physical structures you need for consciousness? This is a very baffling suggestion. In fact, the history of scientifically explaining mental states has mostly done so in terms of computational functions.

Note that the argument that Burns has given is a fully general argument for thinking every biological process needs biology. If we should deny machine consciousness because science methodologically assumes that things require biology, should we have assumed, prior to inventing airplanes, that flight needs biology? Similarly, before the advent of LLMs, should we have assumed that cogent text production needed biology?

As best I can tell, this argument only works if we equivocate between “organic” and “natural.” But those are not the same thing and methodological points that are plausible when applied to the natural world are totally incredible when applied to the organic world. Science does study the natural world, it does not only study the organic world. Elsewhere, Burns elaborates:

This particular claim —that is, responding that computational functionalism is likely false is one that needs to be ‘established’ — is an instance of what I have called in previous work ‘the perversion of the new silicon science’.

As I recently argued, the assumption that those who believe consciousness is biological need to prove this point has the science completely backwards. There are basic methodological precepts that exist in science for a reason: they have proven highly successful. Assuming that natural phenomena arise from organic matter is one of those precepts.

This is wrong on two counts. First, lots of natural phenomena don’t arise from organic matter. For example, planets are natural, but they don’t arise from organic matter. Second, these theories have been successful primarily by suggesting that biology is one of the things that gives rise to natural phenomena, not the only possible thing. There aren’t that many natural properties that can only arise from biology.

If this methodological constraint was correct, at best it would show that biology is one of the things that gives rise to consciousness, just as, across many other sciences, we often think biology gives rise to all sorts of other physical properties. But it would not show that ONLY biology gives rise to consciousness. Certainly it is not taken as a basic principle of science that only biology can give rise to natural properties.

So it seems that Ellen Burns’ master argument for AI insentience is unconvincing. This is a more common trend I’ve found among those who are confident that you need biology for consciousness. While they are often quite confident in their views, when I peek under the hood at their arguments, I find them to have very little weight. There is no good argument for being very confident that you need biology to have a mind.

item.title: Does Christianity Make Sense?
item.description: Reviewing Gavin Ortlund’s book. Or, more precisely, using the excuse of reviewing Gavin Ortlund’s book to provide a comprehensive deep dive into the all the main arguments for Christianity.
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

1 Introduction

My friend Gavin Ortlund has a new book out called Why Christianity Makes Sense, with the subtitle: A Book About Jesus, the Mysteries of the World, and the Longings in Your Heart. He was generous enough to send me an advance copy of the book, which I planned to review—I read it, enjoyed it, then sort of forgot about it for a while before I wrote the review. So here, after much embarrassing delay, is my review.

The book is pretty standard fare for Gavin. A major theme that he likes to emphasize is that Christianity isn’t just true but makes for an awesome story. Everyone should hope that it’s true, even those who think it isn’t. Christianity possesses the three chief transcendentals: truth, beauty, and goodness—showing the goodness and the beauty of Christianity can help a person be receptive to its truth.

The book is good at drawing out the awesomeness of the Christian story. More than once when reading the book, I found myself thinking “what an awesome worldview.” But I’m not a Christian—while I found Gavin’s arguments for Christianity being good and beautiful persuasive, I was not ultimately moved by the arguments for it being true.

There’s a lot to like about the book. If you’re a Christian, I recommend it—if only because, when reading the book, you will more than once be struck with the awesomeness of Christianity. It is also very well written, both clear and engaging. I sailed through it quite quickly. And it provides a good explanation of the central arguments for thinking Christianity is true. The book is a very good encapsulation of the injunction in 1 Peter 3:15 “Always be ready to make your defence to anyone who demands from you an account of the hope that is in you.”

My view, however, is that the arguments for Christianity in the book are unsound.

2 Meaning and hope

Gavin’s first chapter opens with extensive commentary on the existentialists. He treats it as a serious possibility, given naturalism, that the world would be devoid of objective meaning. I’ve never found this persuasive. I don’t quite know what the phrase “objective meaning,” is supposed to mean or why it’s a problem that there isn’t any of it. So long as there’s objective value—objective reasons to perform actions or refrain from them—who cares whether there’s objective meaning? Actions being good or bad is meaning enough.

Chapter 2 discusses how awesome it would be if Christianity is true. Gavin compares belief in Christianity to the experience of Lucy, in the Chronicles of Narnia, going through the wardrobe and discovering a new magical land of wondrous things. This is a good comparison. If Christianity, or theism more broadly, is true, the world is enchanted. You will see your loved ones again, everything dreadful in the world will be undone, “everything sad is going to come untrue” (setting aside thorny issues about hell).

If Christianity is true, then one day, you will meet God himself in an indestructible body. Those who are “in Christ,” at the very least, will then live forever in paradise with the infinite being who made the world, counts every hair on your head, and loves you. That’s pretty cool!

Whether you think Christianity is true or not, it is important enough if true—big iff true—that it makes sense to investigate it carefully. So let’s do that.

3 Does God exist?

Answer: yes.

Unsurprisingly, Gavin agrees. He dedicates several chapters to defending the existence of God. These chapters were interesting, but because they were for a relatively popular audience, he couldn’t explore the arguments in as much detail as I would have liked (note: this isn’t a criticism—I’m not the typical reader).

The first argument he presents is the contingency argument. The basic idea goes: there are lots of contingent things, which could have been otherwise. Something that’s contingent needs explaining. You need an explanation for why it exists instead of not existing. Even if the chain of contingent things is infinite, the infinite chain itself would still cry out for explanation. As an analogy, if there is an infinite chain of cars, each pulled by the one in front of it, and they start suddenly moving, even if every one is pulled by the one in front of it, you still need an explanation of why they started moving. Thus, we should think there’s some necessary being.

Gavin suggests that God is the best candidate for what could end the regress. God, as classically conceived, is the very same thing as his existence. Once you know what kind of thing God is, there isn’t a further question about whether God exists. It doesn’t make sense to ask for an explanation for God, because God is definitionally uncaused. And God is a better candidate for existing than the universe, because the universe is contingent. It could have been otherwise. It’s conceivable that the universe not exist at all.

I’m a bit dubious about these kinds of arguments. For one, I’m pretty okay admitting brute facts into my ontology. Sure, it’s a bit weird that there’s a contingent thing without an explanation, but it doesn’t seem much more mysterious than God existing without explanation. In fact, it seems to make a lot more sense for contingent things to exist without an explanation than for necessary things to exist without an explanation.

Every other necessary truth can be deduced a priori. If you’re clever enough, you can figure out all of mathematics, everything about morality, and so on. This thesis is called modal rationalism, and I accept it. But God’s existence doesn’t seem like the kind of thing that you could figure out a priori, the way you can derive the right answer to a math problem. I also find the idea that God is identical to his existence to be totally incomprehensible!

The theist’s best reply, in my view, is to suggest that God’s existence really can be deduced a priori—we’re just not smart enough to do it. Perhaps, as Aquinas suggested, if we could see more deeply, we’d be able to see that God simply must exist. But I don’t know how this would work and to me it doesn’t seem like any concrete entity has to exist. Anytime some entity’s existence is mysterious, it’s always an option to say that its existence can be derived a priori—we’re just not equipped to do this derivation.

If there is something necessary, must it be God? I think God is a pretty good guess for what the necessary thing would be. A limitless necessary thing is a lot more plausible than a limited necessary thing, just like it seems way more plausible that it would be necessary that empty space is infinite in size than that it’s 8 trillion meters across. So this would raise the probability that God exists, without guaranteeing God’s existence. For example, I could imagine it being necessary that, say, every mathematical structure is concretely instantiated.

So by my reckoning, the contingency argument has some force, but it’s not decisive. If there’s a necessary element of causal reality, it’s probably God. But it’s not clear that there is such an element.

The next section is on the fine-tuning argument. Unsurprisingly, I agreed with most of it. The one bit that I disagreed with concerns the multiverse. Gavin suggests that the multiverse hypothesis is defective because it’s complicated. He says “the multiverse hypothesis seems almost the pinnacle instance of violating Ockham’s razor.”

But simplicity is a matter of the complexity of fundamental entities—those entities that aren’t explained by anything further. For example, suppose that God resolves to flip a coin and create a giant chorus of angels of different kinds if it comes up heads. Should we think, on grounds of simplicity, that it will come up tails? No. Theism posits one fundamental thing: God. All the rest of the complexity falls out of that one simple posit.

Similarly, multiverse theories posit one fundamental thing: some mechanism that generates many universes. This leads to a lot of universes, but it’s not complex, because they all follow from one fundamental entity. If you want to see my preferred reply to the multiverse hypothesis, see here and here.

The next chapter is on the moral argument. I’ve already written a piece about my thoughts on this argument, largely in response to Gavin, so I’ll just link my piece for those interested.

4 Liar, lunatic, legend, lord?

After Gavin finishes arguing for God’s existence, he turns to Christ, arguing that Jesus is God and rose from the dead. Unsurprisingly, this is the part that I buy less.

He begins by presenting the liar, lord, lunatic argument. Now, I agree that this argument has some force. Jesus seems to be less obviously scandal-plagued than, say, Muhammad and Joseph Smith—and he also has a kind of unique compellingness. Similarly, I don’t think the legend option will do completely. Sure, maybe Jesus didn’t claim to be God (I think probably he didn’t claim to be God) but all the first three Gospels attest that Jesus told people to eat bread and drink wine which he said were his flesh and his blood. This is one of the more widely settled facts in the New Testament. A person who suggests that is either depraved, a madman, or God.

The Gospels are littered with instances of Jesus making quite grand pronouncements that would be absurd for anyone other than God to claim. Matthew 16:27 declares “For the Son of Man is going to come in his Father’s glory with his angels, and then he will reward each person according to what they have done.” If someone at the local Wallgreens claimed that he was going to reward each person according to what they’ve done when he comes with the Father’s glory and his angels, you wouldn’t think that they were a sincerely mistaken man of sound mind.

In my view, the best option is a mixture of lunatic and legend.

Jesus must have been at least moderately out to lunch. Of course, lunacy comes in degrees—and people in those days were a lot more willing to make mad-sounding religious claims—but given that Jesus told people to eat bread and drink wine as his flesh and blood, if he was not God, he cannot have been wholly sane. Gavin argues against this on grounds that Jesus is compelling—but many people are both compelling and more than a bit crazy.

I don’t think that Jesus really claimed to be God. So the kind of lunacy he’d have needed to possess is one that compels one to make unbelievable religious claims. Read, for example, the book of Amos. He seemed a bit out to lunch. Maybe Jesus was similarly out to lunch as Amos? Many people throughout history have done this without being visibly raving mad.

Interlude: did Jesus claim to be God

Gavin then turns to some discussion of whether Jesus claimed to be God. My best guess is that he did not, though he had some heightened self-conception. I think John believed that Jesus was God in some sense, but I don’t think that’s true of the synoptics nor of Jesus. Here are some arguments for this:

  1. The synoptics are never clear and explicit that Jesus is God. If Jesus claimed to be God, and that was the most important theme, then probably it would be mentioned clearly and explicitly. Instead, we get ambiguous hints and whispers. Now, you might object that John is somewhat less clear than we’d expect. But I think that John is still reasonably clear, and I also think it’s plausible that the author of John wasn’t totally clear on the sense in which Jesus was divine. It doesn’t seem like the theme of Christianity—that God became man—is that clear in John.

  2. In Mark 10:18, a man calls Jesus good. Jesus totally pwns this guy: “Why do you call me good?” “No one is good—except God alone.” The plain reading of this is that he’s denying that he’s God. Sure, it’s possible that he was subtly hinting at his being God, but this is a less natural reading. Note that Matthew 19:17 tells a conflicting version, where Jesus replies “Why do you ask me about what is good?” The version in Matthew poses less of a problem, but is less historically reliable, as it was probably based on the version in Mark.

  3. Mark 13:32 declares “But about that day or hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.” If Jesus is an omniscient God, then this statement is false! Now, in my view, the best reply is that Jesus was describing the limitations of knowledge in his human form. But still, if you’re an omniscient person, and there’s a third omniscient person too, it’s a bit weird to say “I don’t know X—ONLY the first omniscient person does.”

  4. On the cross, Jesus famously laments “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” How could God forsake God? Now, again, this isn’t definitive. It’s not clear historically that Jesus really said this (it might be an attempt by later writers to draw theological parallels, given the quotation of Psalm 22). And it might be that insofar as Jesus is to suffer the ultimate torment on the cross, he must suffer it, in some deep sense, alone. But I submit that if you are God, it is odd to complain about God forsaking you.

  5. Matthew 12:32 says “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.” This seems to indicate that the Holy Spirit and the Son are not divine in the same way. Note that the action—speaking against, in Greek εἴπῃ κατὰ—is the same. The only difference is who it’s applied to (and, when applied to the Son, there’s an extra word λόγον which means “a word.” But presumably that’s not relevant to its status). Now, there are ways to accommodate this: it could be that when you speak against the Son, that’s forgivable, because you don’t know that he’s God—but turning away from God is unforgivable. Still, it seems to naturally suggest a picture where Jesus and the Spirit are very different kinds of things. It also lends some credence to an anti-trinitarian picture where Jesus is a mode of God, rather than a distinct person—for if the Spirit is a distinct person, it is a bit mysterious that the Father is left out.

  6. Mark 6:5 says, “he could do no deed of power there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and cured them.” God is limitless in power, so this is puzzling if Jesus is God. Note that Matthew 13:58 changes this to “he did not do many miracles there because of their lack of faith.” This fits well with Matthew having a somewhat higher Christology than Mark.

  7. Jesus prays in many places. If Jesus is God, it’s a bit puzzling that he prays to God. Not so if he’s just a man.

What of Gavin’s positive case? Gavin cites Mark 2, where Jesus tells a paralytic that his sins are forgiven. The scribes accuse him of blasphemy, saying “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” In response, Jesus says:

9 Which is easier: to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Stand up and take your mat and walk’? 10 But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic— 11 “I say to you, stand up, take your mat, and go to your home.” 12 And he stood up and immediately took the mat and went out before all of them, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this!”

So Jesus’s reply is to say: if I can heal this guy, then surely I can forgive his sins. He then heals the guy, illustrating that he can forgive sins. Gavin provides the following analogy: suppose a boy’s Father shows up and says “My son, I love you.” The son replies “why are you calling me your son and saying you love me? Only a father can do that.” The father replies “so that you may know that I have authority to call you my son, here’s my DNA and a birth certificate.”

But this is crucially disanalogous. In context, the only way that DNA and a birth certificate might bear on whether it’s legitimate for the man to call the boy “son” is by indicating fatherhood. In contrast, Jesus appeals to his being the son of man, which might give an alternative route to being allowed to forgive sins.

The son of man is a pretty significant figure. Daniel depicts him coming on the clouds of heaven and being given everlasting dominion! So a plausible alternative reading is that Jesus is saying that being the son of man is sufficient to give one the right to forgive sins. You don’t have to be God to forgive sins.

Returning to the earlier example, suppose that the man’s reply was “but I knew you ever since you were just born.” This reply is more analogous, because it involves appealing to possession of some other trait that might be independently sufficient for performing the act in question. But in this case, it would seem like the person was denying being the boy’s father.

Gavin addresses the objection that Jesus says “your sins are forgiven,” rather than “I forgive your sins.” Priests could declare sins forgiven, so maybe Jesus is claiming something more like a priestly prerogative. But Gavin notes that this appears in a passage objecting to the claim that he’s being blasphemous. If Jesus was really declaring the legitimacy of some ordinary priestly prerogative, plausibly he would have replied that the action didn’t require much authority, rather than that he had the requisite authority.

I think this is a good response, but this distinction blunts the force of the argument somewhat. If other actors could declare sins forgiven, then Jesus doing it looks less like a claim to unique divinity. This is strengthened by Matthew 9:8 which declares “When the crowd saw this, they were filled with awe; and they praised God, who had given such authority to man.” Now, possibly this is just reporting on the crowd’s misconception, but in context, it seems pretty misleading.

Gavin next cites the trial of Jesus. Jesus is asked in Matthew 26: “are you the Messiah, the son of God?” The reply:

64 Jesus said to him, “You have said so. But I tell you, From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.” 65 Then the high priest tore his clothes and said, “He has blasphemed! Why do we still need witnesses? You have now heard his blasphemy.

In Mark 14:61, Jesus is asked “Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?” Jesus replies: “I am; and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.”

I think it’s very plausible that Jesus was claiming to be the Messiah and the son of man. But that’s very different from claiming to be God.

Gavin asks why Jesus was being crucified and accused by the Sanhedrin of blasphemy if he wasn’t claiming to be God? Bart Ehrman answers this well in How Jesus Became God: he was accused of claiming to be king of the Jews. After all, in Mark 15:2, Pilate asks Jesus if he’s king of the Jews. Matthew 27:37 adds “Above his head they placed the written charge against him: This is Jesus, the King of the Jews.” And it’s not a charge that Christians would have made up, because king of the Jews isn’t a standard Christian title for Jesus.

This also makes perfect sense of Jesus’s crucifixion. The Romans were happy with the Jews having all sorts of religious beliefs, so long as they demonstrated adequate fealty to Caesar and were subordinate. Claiming a religious title wouldn’t disrupt that. Claiming a juridical title, however, would. Ehrman additionally notes that there are various parallels:

At the end of his life Apollonius was brought up on charges before the emperor Domitian. Among other things, he was accused of receiving the worship that is due only to the gods. Again, the parallels to the story of Jesus are patent: he too was brought before officials (in his case, the leaders of the Jews and then the Roman governor Pilate) and was said to have entertained exalted views of himself, calling himself the Son of God and the king of the Jews. In both cases the officials were persuaded that these claims of self-exaltation were a threat to the well-being of the state, and for both men, readers were assured that in fact these self-claims were completely justified.

This explains why the Romans would crucify Jesus. But why would the priests think he was blaspheming? The answer is that Jesus claimed to be the Danielic Son of Man who would ascend on the clouds of heaven. That’s certainly not the least blasphemous statement I ever heard! It’s also plausible that the scene isn’t historical, and bears little resemblance to Jesus’s actual crucifixion.

Gavin argues that Romans 9:5 indicates that the earliest Christians worshipped Jesus as God. Now, the grammar of Romans 9:5 is a bit unclear, but I think probably Paul was saying that Jesus is God. On my view, Paul thought that Jesus was divine in some sense, but I find it hard to know what Paul was saying. Here are my main reasons for thinking this:

  1. Romans 1: 3-4 says: “his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and designated Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.” This seems to indicate that Jesus was designated Son of God by the resurrection.

  2. 1 Corinthians 11:3 says “But I want you to understand that Christ is the head of every man, and the husband is the head of his wife, and God is the head of Christ.” This seems to indicate Jesus being subordinate to God, as humans are subordinate to Christ. Now, some object that “head” can mean cause or source of. But this reading seems a bit tortured. Is the husband the source of his wife? This is buttressed by 1 Corinthians 15:28: “When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who put all things in subjection under him, so that God may be all in all.” And 1 Corinthians 3:23 says “you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.”

  3. 1 Corinthians 8:6 says “there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.” This seems to indicate that God is the Father, not a trinity, and he is distinct from the one Lord.

  4. Outside of Romans 9:5 and the disputed letters, Paul reserves the title God (Theos) for the Father and lord (Kyrios) for the son.

One of the most common pro-divinity passages is Philippians 2 (important lines for both sides of the debate bolded):

6 who, though he existed in the form of God,
did not regard equality with God
as something to be grasped,
7 but emptied himself,
taking the form of a slave,
assuming human likeness.
And being found in appearance as a human,
8 he humbled himself
and became obedient to the point of death—
even death on a cross.

9 Therefore God exalted him even more highly
and gave him the name
that is above every other name,
10 so that at the name given to Jesus
every knee should bend,
 in heaven and on earth and under the earth,
11 and every tongue should confess
that Jesus Christ is Lord,
to the glory of God the Father.

This passage is confusing. On the one hand, it seems to indicate Jesus’s glory being derivative through God. It talks about God exalting him even more highly. On the other hand, it talks about Jesus being “in the form of God,” and mentions that at the name given to him “every knee should bend.” This references the declaration in Isaiah 45 that every knee will bow before God.

Here’s my guess as to Paul’s view: Jesus was a pre-existing celestial being who, through God’s participation, was taken up and elevated, so that he was divine in some important sense. This has precedent: 2 Corinthians 8:9 says “For you know the generous act of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.” In my view, this is the best explanation of all the passages in question: both the ones that indicate Jesus’s subordination to the Father, his derivative divinity, and the ones that speak of him being God in some important sense. This also explains why Jesus could be worshipped and why various other passages indicate his elevated status.

In addition, even if Paul claimed that Jesus is God, this wouldn’t necessarily mean Jesus had said it. It seems that Christology was hotly debated in early Christian communities. It may be that Paul had high Christology while later authors had low Christology.

Overall, then, my read of the evidence is that Jesus probably didn’t claim to be God. I don’t think this totally defeats the liar, lunatic, lord argument, but it’s strong independent evidence against Christianity. It also weakens the liar, lunatic, lord argument, by lowering the extent of Jesus’s personal pronouncements.

5 Did Jesus rise from the dead?

If he did, that would be a big deal!

We know the early Christians said that they saw Jesus posthumously. One explanation of why you might say that you saw a guy after he died is if you really did see him after he died. And Gavin argues convincingly that the early Christians were sincere—otherwise they wouldn’t risk serious persecution.

I agree that Jesus’s disciples claimed to see him posthumously. But I think in charged religious settings, you can pretty easily get a lot of impressive claims swirling around about witnessed miracles. The early Mormon witnesses claimed see Golden plates—though I think probably there were not golden plates—and claimed to hear an angel of God declare the revelation to be genuine.
