Or take Sathya Sai Baba, an Indian spiritual leader and obvious fraudster. It’s clear he’s a fraudster from both videos and the testimony of those around him. He does cheap magic tricks that fool people. has a nice article going over some of the testimonies concerning Sai Baba. Some examples:

Baba gave me a rather flat stone of irregular size and asked me to throw it up in the air. I threw it high up, and he asked me to catch it when it came down. I was afraid the stone might hurt my hands. By the time I caught it, it was an apple. I gave the apple to Swami, who took a knife and cut it into pieces, and everyone present got a piece of the size into which we normally cut apples. From this one apple he gave pieces to some 25 people. This was a medium-size apple; normally it might have sufficed for 8 to 10 people.

…

At lunchtime - about 12.00 or 12.30 - he asked everybody to bring empty vessels. I saw this incident clearly and with my own eyes, so I can't forget it. Baba just made a movement with his hand right over the empty vessels, and I could see the food rising up from the bottom! I would say that he produced about a dozen varieties of dishes in this way, one in each vessel, and it came up in a matter of seconds .. .. Then Baba told us: 'This is why I told you not to prepare any food. I was intending to give you something divine, prasadam.

…

On many occasions, especially when we were walking by the river, he would suddenly vanish from sight. As he vanished, he would be walking with us in a group and talking to us. We would not see him or find him. But then he would be calling me or someone by name, and when you looked for him you would find that he would be at the top of the mountain (hill). All this would happen within seconds.

…

Another devotee explained how he had begun as a skeptic, and gone to see Sai Baba out of curiosity. On the way, the bus briefly broke down, but was fixed and the journey continued. Later on, the man and his party had to cross a riverbed on foot, and he carried his little cousin’s violin in his hand. When he got to Puttaparthi, Sai Baba described to him exactly how the bus had broken down, including the town where it had done so, and how he had to carry his cousin’s violin across the river.

One could multiply examples: young children claimed to see Mary even when it’s clear they didn’t, 62 children who claimed to see a UFO, groups of Piraha who claim to see spirits in real time, and much more. People really can report seeing crazy things that they didn’t see. For this reason, I don’t place that much weight in the resurrection reports.

Gavin places a lot of weight on the fact that we have hostile witness testimony from Paul and James. James didn’t believe in Jesus’s ministry and Paul was an active persecutor of the Church. But this sort of thing is relatively common. The above case depicts a Sai Baba skeptic who was won over by the impressive miracles. In Islam, the second caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab, was originally a persecutor of Muslims—won over, supposedly, after hearing the Quran. Ummar even tried to kill Muhammed, if the stories are to be believed!

What about the fact that the stories depict appearances in groups? Again, the miracles attributed to Sai Baba, the ones concerning UFOs, and the golden plates depict events that occurred in groups.

One other thing that strikes me as strange is the repeated emphasis on the doubting of the disciples even after the resurrection. In Luke 24, the disciples don’t recognize him for a while. Matthew 28 describes that “some doubted.” This seems more expected if he didn’t really rise and the authors are attempting to explain those who didn’t see him.

Gavin argues that Jesus was buried in a tomb. I’m not totally sure about this, but I think it was probably right. The best argument for the burial is that it’s attested in our two earliest sources: 1 Corinthians 15:3 and the Gospel of Mark. 1 Corinthians 15:3 quotes a creed that dates to just after the crucifixion and says “Christ died for our sins, as the scriptures said he would; that he was buried and rose again on the third day, again as the scriptures foretold.” And as Dale Allison writes:

According to the old confession in 1 Cor. 15:4, Jesus “died” and “was buried” (ἐτάφη). The first meaning of the verb, θάπτω, is “honor with funeral rites, especially by burial” (LSJ, s.v.). Nowhere in Jewish sources, furthermore, does the formula, “died…and was buried,” refer to anything other than interment in the ground, a cave, or a tomb. So the language of the pre-Pauline formula cannot have been used of a body left to rot on a cross.

Ultimately, I don’t really know whether Jesus was buried. I think there are a few possibilities:

  1. Jesus was thrown in a mass grave.

  2. Jesus was left on the cross.

  3. Jesus was buried in a special tomb reserved for criminals.

  4. Jesus was temporarily stored in a tomb and then reburied.

  5. Jesus was left in a tomb, as the Gospels describe.

I find the 1 Corinthians creed to be a strong consideration against 2. For reasons I’ve laid out here, I find the arguments for 2 pretty weak. The ones I have the highest credence in are 5, 1, and 3. It seems that burial in a mass grave was a common Roman procedure, though counting against it is that the Jews didn’t like it. And it makes sense that Christians would retcon that embarrassing detail.

I don’t find Markan attestation to the burial to be very strong evidence. Mark was writing more than thirty years later. It’s not that surprising that a story like that would develop, especially given that the Gospels grow increasingly grand in their proclamations about Jesus’s burial. Mark describes Jesus being buried in a tomb which had been hewn out of the rock, while Matthew makes it his own new tomb, while Luke adds that it’s a tomb where nobody had ever been laid. Matthew also adds a guard at the tomb. Joseph of Arimathea’s closeness to Jesus also grows.

The chapter doesn’t discuss the empty tomb in detail, though it does discuss the burial (see here for my thoughts on the empty tomb). Maybe the idea is that once you grant the burial an empty tomb would be hard to deny? If the tomb was full, then the body could have been wheeled out and the early Christian movement would have been crushed. But this is hard to say. People are pretty irrational! There are all sorts of conspiracy theories that people believe in today which seem like they wouldn’t survive a google search. Or maybe people didn’t know where the tomb was. Public preaching, according to acts, started 7 weeks later, when a body would have been hard to identify.

What about the argument that the attestation by the women would have been inexplicable unless they were telling the truth? Patriarchal Jewish society devalued the testimony of women. They weren’t taken seriously in courts. Four main problems:

  1. In the story, Jesus’s disciples had abandoned him. So the women were the only ones left to witness it.

  2. This is undercut by the lack of agreement about which women were at the tomb. Mark says it was “Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome,” Matthew has just the two Marys, Luke said the women were “Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles,” while John just includes Mary Magdalene.

  3. Women were naturally entrusted with mourning the dead. So it makes sense that they’d be found at the tomb.

  4. While women’s testimony was generally not counted in court, they were still often taken seriously as the source of eyewitness reports.

Alternatively, this just means that if you doubt the empty tomb, you should also doubt the burial. Given that the arguments for the burial aren’t knock-down, this gives a reason for those antecedently skeptical of Christianity to doubt the burial.

6 General thoughts on prophecy

Gavin’s eighth chapter is about the argument from prophecy. He claims that Jesus’s coming was prophesied ahead of time for centuries by specific prophetic predictions.

Gavin emphasizes that the argument from prophecy has its weight cumulatively. Sure, maybe any individual prophecy can be explained away as good luck. But the sheer number of them is hard to explain. I disagree. When you have a text that is long and unspecific, and later narratives are crafted in light of the earliest texts, it isn’t surprising that there’s a lot of correspondence between the texts.

Probably the best example is Scott Alexander’s article My Antichrist Lecture. In it, he tries to match up lines from the book of revelation with modern AI development. There are many details that match up cumulatively—for example:

  • “[The Beast] had power to give life unto the image of the beast, that the image of the beast should speak.” That sounds a lot like LLM development.

  • The Beast has seven heads. Anthropic has seven cofounders.

  • It says that on the heads will be names of blasphemy. Scott goes through and provides ways of identifying each of the Anthropic cofounders as blasphemous.

  • The antichrist is supposedly going to be disguised with the title of Christ. Christ is called the Alpha and the Omega. A16Z is literally the Alpha and the Omega.

  • “Google says that the most common name meaning “son of man” is “Anderson”, from Greek “Andreas” + son. And Silicon Valley’s most powerful venture capitalist is named Marc Andreessen.”

  • “In what sense is Marc Andreessen a “horn with human eyes”? Here, as before, I think it helps to try being as literal as possible:”

The details continue. Some are no longer applicable (e.g. Scott talks about how the number of the beast being 666 corresponds with Anthropic being the only AI company to have between 500 and 1000 employees—but now it has a lot more). I was impressed by seeing how many parallels he was able to draw. Similar things are true of prophecies of Nostradamus (though I find those to be generally less impressive than Scott’s examples).

Or take the Simpsons as another example. People often talk about how accurately the Simpsons predict the future. Simpsons episodes depict:

  • Trump being president (the episode came out in the year 2,000).

  • Disney buying fox.

  • Bengt Holmström’s Nobel prize.

And various other things. It just seems surprisingly easy to proliferate specific correct predictions in a large corpus of unspecific text. Or, to take another example, if you ever watch the videos of The Film Theorists where he argues jokingly for crazy theories about movies—like that Wall-E involves cannibalism—he’s able to muster a surprising number of facts in support of it. It’s just easy to find coincidences.

So for this reason, I’m pretty initially skeptical of the arguments from fulfilled prophecy. I just don’t know how many prophecies of Jesus you’d be able to squeeze out of a text like the Bible. Then, add one additional fact: all of the prophecies have alternative readings.

For example, three of the best prophecies in the Old Testament are Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, and Wisdom 2 (Gavin focuses primarily on Isaiah 53 and doesn’t mention Wisdom 2—which isn’t surprising because it’s not in Protestant Bibles and he’s a Protestant). But each of these have other readings: Psalm 22 is plausibly just a generic lamentation, Wisdom 2 is making a general statement about evildoers, and Isaiah 53 is has an alternative reading about Israel.

If there were prophecies about Jesus, I’d expect it to be pretty clear that they were foretelling of a coming person. If there were genuine specific prophecies of Jesus in the Old Testament, I wouldn’t expect there to be, in each case, plausible alternative readings so that you have to do subtle in-the-weeds textual exegesis to figure out what it’s about.

Gavin argues that the central theme of the Old Testament is God choosing to bless the world through a specific individual who is variously spoken of as both a king and a priest. But Jesus was, on his face, neither obviously a king nor a priest. He was only interpreted this way due to the prophecies. So this seems like a classic example of a self-fulfilling prophecy—the Christian conception of Jesus was shaped by Old Testament prophecies.

Gavin argues that the Old Testament seems to depict the Messiah as both a triumphant king and lowly servant. For this, he cites Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, and Zechariah 9:9. I don’t think Psalm 22 was Messianic. Psalm 22 reads (only quoting the relevant bit):

scorned by others and despised by the people.

they sneer at me; they shake their heads;

12 Many bulls encircle me;
strong bulls of Bashan surround me;

and all my bones are out of joint;
my heart is like wax;
it is melted within my breast;
15 my mouth[a] is dried up like a potsherd,
and my tongue sticks to my jaws;
you lay me in the dust of death.

16 For dogs are all around me;
a company of evildoers encircles me;
they bound my hands and feet.[b]
17 I can count all my bones.
They stare and gloat over me;
18 they divide my clothes among themselves,
and for my clothing they cast lots.

19 But you, O Lord, do not be far away!
O my help, come quickly to my aid!
20 Deliver my soul from the sword,
my life[c] from the power of the dog!

From the horns of the wild oxen you have rescued[d] me.
22 I will tell of your name to my brothers and sisters;[e]
in the midst of the congregation I will praise you:

So the specific claims seem to be:

  1. The person in question is a worm and not a man.

  2. The people who see him mock him and say “Commit your cause to the Lord; let him deliver—let him rescue the one in whom he delights!”

  3. He’s surrounded by lions and bulls.

  4. He’s “poured out like water.”

  5. His bones are out of joint.

  6. His “heart is like wax.”

  7. His mouth is dry.

  8. His hands and feet are either bound or pierced depending on the translation.

  9. His clothes are divided up by casting lots.

Which of these are plausibly true of Jesus? 1 seems false—Jesus is a man and not a worm. In response to this, my friend points out that word for worm is תּוֹלַ֧עַת, which can mean the scarlet grub. This is the same word, for example, that appears in Isaiah 1:18, to mean red. Still, I don’t find this to be that impressive (more in a footnote).1 It seems like the kind of attempt to post hoc match up details that you’d get from a non-genuine prophecy.

2 is likely added to fulfill the prophecy. 3 is false as literally stated. It’s not totally clear what 4 means. 5 is unclear because during crucifixion bones generally aren’t out of joint (or so Claude tells me). 6 is ambiguous. 7 is plausibly fulfilled but not that impressive. 8 is debatable and depends on translation. But the fact that a text that makes a bunch of predictions gets right that Jesus had a dry mouth and maybe that he was pierced isn’t that impressive. 9 is very likely intentional fulfillment.

7 Isaiah 53

What about Isaiah 53, which Gavin discusses at much greater length? Let’s go through it piece by piece, starting with Isaiah 52.

13 See, my servant shall prosper;
he shall be exalted and lifted up
and shall be very high.

14 Just as there were many who were astonished at him[c] —so marred was his appearance, beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of mortals— 15 so he shall startle[d] many nations; kings shall shut their mouths because of him, for that which had not been told them they shall see, and that which they had not heard they shall contemplate.

This doesn’t seem like a perfect match for Jesus. Jesus started out high, rather than being exalted. In fact, the general picture is that he went from being high to low. To quote a sentence from C.S. Lewis—which is maybe the best sentence I’ve ever read:

The total pattern, of which they are only the turning point, is the real Death and Re-birth: for certainly no seed ever fell from so fair a tree into so dark and cold a soil as would furnish more than a faint analogy to this huge descent and re-ascension in which God dredged the salt and oozy bottom of Creation.

Now, it’s not strictly contradictory or anything. But it’s a somewhat weird way to talk about Jesus. If God became a man, it’s odd to describe this as someone being lifted up. Jesus’s scourging before the crucifixion would involve him being marred. It is true that some kings “shut their mouths because of him,” in at least the minimal sense that they were surprised by the message of the Gospel. But this is not very specific.

53 Who has believed what we have heard? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? 2 For he grew up before him like a young plant and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, nothing in his appearance that we should desire him. 3 He was despised and rejected by others; a man of suffering[a] and acquainted with infirmity, and as one from whom others hide their faces[b] he was despised, and we held him of no account.

The stuff about him having “no form of majesty that we should look at him,” seems like little evidence either way, as it’s not really spoken to in the Gospels. Jesus was rejected by some people, but he was also followed by many.

4 Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our diseases, yet we accounted him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted. 5 But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed. 6 All we like sheep have gone astray; we have all turned to our own way, and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. 7 He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he did not open his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he did not open his mouth.

This does bear some similarities to atonement theology. But the theology of the atonement was crafted with passages like Isaiah 53 in mind. The term that’s translated as “for our” can also mean “from our.” In addition, vicarious satisfaction appears elsewhere in the Bible—in Ezekiel 4:4, Ezekiel is told to lie on his side for days to bear the sin of Israel. Isaiah 40:2 also depicts Israel paying a penalty for her sins. So the correspondence isn’t that surprising. A bunch of kind of vague metaphors about suffering for the sake of others aren’t very impressive or specific.

8 By a perversion of justice he was taken away.
Who could have imagined his future?
For he was cut off from the land of the living,
stricken for the transgression of my people.
9 They made his grave with the wicked
and his tomb[c] with the rich,[d]
although he had done no violence,
and there was no deceit in his mouth.

10 Yet it was the will of the Lord to crush him with affliction.
When you make his life an offering for sin,[e]
he shall see his offspring and shall prolong his days;
through him the will of the Lord shall prosper.

The line about his grave being with the rich might be a reference to Joseph of Arimathea. But I’m skeptical that really happened. In fact, Joseph may have been an invention to fulfill the prophecy. Additionally, some translations say he was with “rich people,” in his death.

So the specific things we have that are evidentially relevant are that he’ll suffer for others, be cut off from the land of the living but still have his days prolonged, and that he’ll suffer for others. The line about how he’ll be stricken for the transgression of “my people” isn’t clear—various other translators say he was stricken because of the transgresions of his people (though this seems to be the minority). These are pretty good parallels, but I don’t know that they’re much better than the base rates of what you’d expect in a text like the Bible.

11 Out of his anguish he shall see; he shall find satisfaction through his knowledge. The righteous one,[f] my servant, shall make many righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities. 12 Therefore I will allot him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out himself to death and was numbered with the transgressors, yet he bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.

Some of these are pretty weird. Did Jesus find satisfaction through his knowledge? It’s also weird to say that Jesus gets allotted a portion with the great because he poured himself to death. If he’s God, then this isn’t why he gets a portion with the great.

But to figure out what Isaiah 53 is about, you should look at the chapters before Isaiah 53. Starting with Isaiah 42, there is extensive discussion of the servant. Isaiah 43:10 says, speaking to the people of Israel, “You are my witnesses, says the Lord,
and my servant whom I have chosen.”

Brief digression—Isaiah 43:20 says:

20 The wild animals will honour me,
the jackals and the ostriches;
for I give water in the wilderness,
rivers in the desert,

That is not relevant to the dispute at hand—it is just very based. Concern for wild animals VINDICATED BY GOD, haters malding.

Okay, back to the point at hand, Isaiah 44 says:

1 But now hear, O Jacob my servant, Israel whom I have chosen! 2 Thus says the Lord who made you, who formed you in the womb and will help you: Do not fear, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen.

So it seems like the servant is Israel. Then Isaiah 44 adds:

21 Remember these things, O Jacob,
and Israel, for you are my servant;
I formed you, you are my servant;
O Israel, you will not be forgotten by me.
22 I have swept away your transgressions like a cloud,
and your sins like mist;
return to me, for I have redeemed you

This reiterates that Israel is the servant. Isaiah 45:4 adds “For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I surname you, though you do not know me.” By Isaiah 46:3, we read “3 Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from your birth, carried from the womb.” Isaiah 48:20 says “The Lord has redeemed his servant Jacob!”

One of the most interesting passages is Isaiah 49 (important bits highlighted):

49 Listen to me, O coastlands,
pay attention, you peoples from far away!
The Lord called me before I was born,
while I was in my mother’s womb he named me.
2 He made my mouth like a sharp sword,
in the shadow of his hand he hid me;
he made me a polished arrow,
in his quiver he hid me away.
3 And he said to me, ‘You are my servant,
Israel, in whom I will be glorified.’
4 But I said, ‘I have laboured in vain,
I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity;
yet surely my cause is with the Lord,
and my reward with my God.’

5 And now the Lord says,
who formed me in the womb to be his servant,
to bring Jacob back to him,
and that Israel might be gathered to him,
for I am honoured in the sight of the Lord,
and my God has become my strength—
6 he says,
‘It is too light a thing that you should be my servant
to raise up the tribes of Jacob
and to restore the survivors of Israel;
I will give you as a light to the nations,
that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.’

I find this passage particularly hard to parse.

My best guess is the passage is talking about Isaiah (or whoever wrote this bit of Isaiah). He suggests that Isaiah (or whoever wrote this part of Isaiah) is supposed to provide teachings that guide both Israel and the surrounding nations. Isaiah 50:10 supports the interpretation that Isaiah is identified as a servant, writing “Who among you fears the Lord and obeys the voice of his servant, who walks in darkness and has no light, yet trusts in the name of the Lord and relies upon his God?” I don’t think this passage is very plausibly about Jesus for the author speaks in first person. It also seems odd that Jesus would say that he had labored in vain.

Daniel 12:3 says “Those who are wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens, and those who lead many to righteousness, like the stars for ever and ever.” This is plausibly a reference to Isaiah and suggests that leading to righteousness isn’t restricted to one suffering servant.

My best guess is that the servant in Isaiah 53 refers to Israel. This nicely explains why there are so many passages that say explicitly that Israel is the servant. Often it’s identified with the righteous remnant in Israel. So talk about the servant suffering to redeem the world can refer either to Israel suffering or the righteous in Israel suffering.

8 Daniel 9, more like Daniel, nein

The next prophecy Gavin turns to is Daniel 9, though he doesn’t discuss it in much detail. Here’s what Daniel 9 says:

24 “Seventy weeks are decreed for your people and your holy city: to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal both vision and prophet, and to anoint a most holy place.[g] 25 Know therefore and understand: from the time that the word went out to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until the time of an anointed prince, there shall be seven weeks, and for sixty-two weeks it shall be built again with streets and moat, but in a troubled time. 26 After the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing, and the troops of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its[h] end shall come with a flood, and to the end there shall be war. Desolations are decreed. 27 He shall make a strong covenant with many for one week, and for half of the week he shall make sacrifice and offering cease, and in their place[i] shall be a desolating sacrilege until the decreed end is poured out upon the desolator.”

This is a confusing passage. Note one feature: “weeks” here refers to number of years. A week is seven years.

Let’s start with the decree to rebuild Jerusalem. When was this?

The most plausible reading, and the one that’s dominant among scholars, is that the word in question refers to the prophecy given to Jeremiah. Note that the chapter starts in verse 2 talking about “the word of the Lord given to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years.” Daniel 9:23 additionally says “As soon as you began to pray, a word went out, which I have come to tell you, for you are highly esteemed. Therefore, consider the word and understand the vision.”

In addition, Jeremiah did prophecy the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Jeremiah seemed to prophesy that Jerusalem would be rebuilt after 70 years, and this gets discussed in other prophetic writings. So the most plausible reading of Daniel 9 is that he’s commenting on Jeremiah—but warning that it will take 7x longer before the temple is rebuilt. Jeremiah died in 582, so if this is about Jeremiah, then it can’t be about Jesus.

In addition, it being about Jeremiah fits well with the dates. From 587 to Cyrus’s decree in 538 is 49 years. So this nicely explains “from the time that the word went out to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until the time of an anointed prince, there shall be seven weeks.” The Jesus reading requires garbling this and running together the seven and sixty two weeks as one statement about sixty nine weeks, which is very weird.

What is the anointing of a most holy place? The standard view, articulated in Collins’ commentary on Daniel, is that this refers to the “rededication of the Jerusalem Temple, which was actually accomplished by Judas Maccabee late in 164.” Note that Daniel is very likely written right around this time, and elsewhere seems to predict the desolation of the temple lasting only a few years (see Daniel 8:14).

Who is the anointed one who gets cut off? This refers to “the murder of the high priest Onias III, recorded in 2 Macc 4:23-28, in about 171.” The prince is Antiochus (who Daniel comments on extensively). The destruction of the city and the sanctuary is the assault on Jerusalem in 167. The desolate sacrifices came from the pagan altar of 167 BCE.

What about the Christian interpretation of this passage? Of the decrees related to the rebuilding of Jerusalem, there were:

  • 538: Ezra 1 describes the Jewish people being allowed to return to Jerusalem and “rebuild the house of the Lord.”2 This wouldn’t line up with the dates.

  • 516: the temple is fully rebuilt, after, in 520, Darius finds Cyrus’s decree in the archives.

  • 458-457: A commission goes to Ezra that says people can freely go to Jerusalem, offers gold and silver to buy animals for sacrifice, and gives Ezra the right to appoint judges. Artaxerxes later halts the work.

  • 445: Nehemiah is permitted to rebuild the walls and gates. He quickly does.

Jesus was crucified in 30 or 33, so the dates only work out if you assume that the “word…to restore and rebuild Jerusalem” refers to the 458-457 Ezra commission. This only works out if Jesus was crucified in 30 (the minority view). Now, it is some coincidence that the dates work out, but there are a lot of degrees of freedom, and the thing that happened in 458 doesn’t really seem like the restoration of Jerusalem. When you have many different prophecies with many different interpretations giving many different dates, it isn’t that surprising that some would line up nicely.

The end of sacrifice appears elsewhere in Daniel. Daniel 11:31 says “Forces sent by him shall occupy and profane the temple and fortress. They shall abolish the regular burnt offering and set up the desolating sacrilege.” This is clearly about Antiochus. So if this end up sacrifice is discussed elsewhere in Daniel, it’s more parsimonious to think this is also what Daniel 9 is about.

Daniel 9:27 says “for half of the week he shall make sacrifice and offering cease, and in their place shall be a desolating sacrilege until the decreed end is poured out upon the desolator.” It’s a bit odd to describe Jesus’s crucifixion as a desolating sacrilege. And Jesus didn’t end sacrifice for half a week (three and a half years). Sacrifices were ended a lot later. Similarly, the line “to the end there shall be war,” doesn’t seem to describe Jesus’s crucifixion. While maybe this could refer to the destruction of the temple, that came a lot later.

In addition, in Daniel 9, events are described as occurring sequentially after the events prophecied in Daniel 9. But the events in Daniel 10 and especially 11 very likely (as I’ve argued here) depict events that were happening around 167.

The best Christian reply is to argue that there was dual fulfillment. Perhaps this can be used both to describe Jesus’s crucifixion and the events around 167. But still, given the disharmonies between the passage and the life of Jesus, and the fact that it is otherwise intelligible in light of the events of 167, this doesn’t seem very compelling.

For this reason, I am not very moved by the prophecy of Daniel 9. At a high level, my earlier comments about each prophecy having a plausible alternative reading seems correct.

9 Slavery

The next section of Gavin’s book is titled “the Bible is good for humanity.” In this section, he argues:

  1. Major moral objections to the Bible fail.

  2. The Bible has significantly advanced humanity’s moral status.

I agree that Christianity has been a force for good in the world. This is well-argued by Tom Holland in his book Dominion. Christianity radically upended the morality of the west in a way that improved it considerably. Nonetheless, there might be powerful moral objections to Christianity even if it’s good all-things-considered. The Code of Hammurabi advanced humanity morally; however, it contains enough serious moral errors for it to be clear it was not from God.

Gavin discusses the Bible’s teachings on slavery, which I find to be powerful evidence against inerrancy. (Self-plagiarism alert—the passages I’m citing are ones I cited before in the linked article). For example, from Leviticus 25:44-46:

“Your male and female slaves are to come from the nations around you; from them you may buy slaves. You may also buy some of the temporary residents living among you and members of their clans born in your country, and they will become your property. You can bequeath them to your children as inherited property and can make them slaves for life, but you must not rule over your fellow Israelites ruthlessly”.

Exodus 21:20-21 adds:

20 “Anyone who beats their male or female slave with a rod must be punished if the slave dies as a direct result, 21 but they are not to be punished if the slave recovers after a day or two, since the slave is their property.

Ephesians 6:5 commands “Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, in singleness of heart, as you obey Christ.” Colossians 3:22 says, “Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything, not only while being watched and in order to please them, but wholeheartedly, fearing the Lord.”

Concerningly, some of the hard passages on slavery come from Jesus himself. Matthew 10:24 reads “A disciple is not above the teacher nor a slave above the master.” Luke 17 has Jesus say:

7 “Who among you would say to your slave who has just come in from plowing or tending sheep in the field, ‘Come here at once and take your place at the table’? 8 Would you not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me; put on your apron and serve me while I eat and drink; later you may eat and drink’? 9 Do you thank the slave for doing what was commanded? 10 So you also, when you have done all that you were ordered to do, say, ‘We are worthless slaves; we have done only what we ought to have done!’ ”

Luke 12 adds:

43 Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives. 44 Truly I tell you, he will put that one in charge of all his possessions. 45 But if that slave says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the other slaves, men and women, and to eat and drink and get drunk, 46 the master of that slave will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour that he does not know and will cut him in pieces[i] and put him with the unfaithful. 47 That slave who knew what his master wanted but did not prepare himself or do what was wanted will receive a severe beating. 48 But the one who did not know and did what deserved a beating will receive a light beating. From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required, and from the one to whom much has been entrusted, even more will be demanded.

Gavin argues that though God opposes slavery, he made affordances to the immoral beliefs at the time, just like how Jesus says God only permitted divorce because of the hardness of the people’s hearts. But God gave all sorts of burdensome teachings. Jesus prohibited divorce, God told the Israelites to get circumcised, and had a billion other burdensome laws. If he could get them to slice off parts of their penis and not wear mixed fabrics, it doesn’t seem like it would have been outside the bounds of the possible for him to suggest that slavery is a lamentable institution—even short of calling for its full abolition. The Essenes, another Jewish sect at the time, apparently opposed slavery.

Gavin suggests that Israelite slavery was less cruel than other institutions of slavery. Certainly it was better in some respects but it was worse in others. When slaves were freed in the seventh year, if they were given a wife, their wives remained enslaved. In addition, Mesopotamian slaves could own property in a limited way—Israelite slaves could not.

Gavin cites 1 Timothy 1:10 as evidence of Paul’s disapproval of slavery. But the standard scholarly view is that Paul didn’t write 1 Timothy.

Lastly, he argues that Christianity made tremendous progress against slavery. The idea that everyone is made in God’s image formed the moral backbone of the case against slavery. If even slaves are in God’s image, then slavery is an abomination. Many Christians recognized this argument.

But holding principles that entail that slavery should be abolished is easy and common. Slavery is evil and violates many obvious moral principles. By default, we should expect a religion to affirm moral judgments that are incompatible with slavery. But throughout history, affirming these kinds of judgments has often existed alongside support for slavery. If Christianity was false, it isn’t very surprising that it would affirm some principles incompatible with slavery. If it was true, it is surprising it would include so many pro-slavery passages. The slavery passages are, therefore, strong evidence against a high view of scripture.

Here’s one final way to see that this must be some evidence at least. Imagine if we learned that the Bible clearly condemned slavery. Maybe there’s some passage that we realized we’d misreading all along. Clearly that would be evidence for Christianity. So then our not finding it is evidence against. If God had a major hand in the crafting of the Bible, it would be surprising that much of its contents look similar to the regressive beliefs of the surrounding culture and time period.

10 Old Testament violence

Points I make here are largely repeats of ones I’ve made here.

Gavin’s next chapter concerns Old Testament violence. Some of the violent passages include Deuteronomy 7:2 “when the Lord your God has delivered them over to you and you have defeated them, then you must destroy them totally. Make no treaty with them, and show them no mercy.”

Gavin suggests that the actions depicted are a just response to the evil of the Canaanites—for example, Deuteronomy 12:31 talks about the Canaanites engaging in child sacrifice. But most societies throughout history have done lots of evil things. I don’t think that licenses total destructive warfare on most societies throughout history. More importantly, the evil of the Canaanites is not the only—or even the primary—justification for driving them out. Passages like Genesis 15 depict the land being owed to the Israelites.

God is omnipotent. He can intervene in the world however he wants. There are numerous things he could have done to eradicate the Canaanites’ evil. So it is surprising that God would intervene in the world in a major way, only to command ethnic cleansing.

More importantly, even if some kind of war was justified, the way it was carried out was not. For example, here is Deuteronomy 20:

10 When you march up to attack a city, make its people an offer of peace. 11 If they accept and open their gates, all the people in it shall be subject to forced labor and shall work for you. 12 If they refuse to make peace and they engage you in battle, lay siege to that city. 13 When the Lord your God delivers it into your hand, put to the sword all the men in it. 14 As for the women, the children, the livestock and everything else in the city, you may take these as plunder for yourselves. And you may use the plunder the Lord your God gives you from your enemies. 15 This is how you are to treat all the cities that are at a distance from you and do not belong to the nations nearby.

16 However, in the cities of the nations the Lord your God is giving you as an inheritance, do not leave alive anything that breathes. 17 Completely destroy[a] them—the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites—as the Lord your God has commanded you. 18 Otherwise, they will teach you to follow all the detestable things they do in worshiping their gods, and you will sin against the Lord your God.

This is not plausibly an example of wartime hyperbole. It is a specific instruction not a depiction of a glorious battle. And it suggests that the Israelites should kill all the men and take all the women and children as “plunder.” Numbers 31:17-18 adds:

Now therefore, kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known a man by sleeping with him. But all the young girls who have not known a man by sleeping with him, keep alive for yourselves.

Joshua 6 adds:

21 They devoted the city to the Lord and destroyed with the sword every living thing in it—men and women, young and old, cattle, sheep and donkeys.

…

24 Then they burned the whole city and everything in it, but they put the silver and gold and the articles of bronze and iron into the treasury of the Lord’s house.

More evidence against the wartime hyperbole hypothesis is 1 Samuel 15 which has a lengthy plotline about Saul sinning by failing to completely wipe out the Amalekites. 1 Samuel 15:2-3 even says that the injunction to destroy the Amalekites is explained by what they did 400 years earlier:

2 Thus says the Lord of hosts: I will punish the Amalekites for what they did in opposing the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt. 3 Now go and attack Amalek and utterly destroy all that they have; do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.”

Even if you think that the injunction to kill the Canaanites was permissible—even if you think that way God did it was better than doing nothing—it is very surprising that the God of the Old Testament seems to be depicted so similarly to tribal war gods of the surrounding time period. put it well:

One issue here is that it’s not *just* that, e.g., the genocide commands seem like something God wouldn’t command; it’s that they *also* seem like the sort of thing Bronze Age people would falsely make up. This is obvious in the case of, say, Mormonism: “all these women need to have sex with Joseph Smith” seems surprising coming from God, but not surprising coming from Joseph Smith. People have claimed divine sanction for war crimes all throughout history, and presumably we both agree that they were almost always wrong; it’s kind of weird if it turns out God really did order genocide a couple times, and it happened to be in a context where everybody thought genocide was cool and good.

Then, lastly, though I admit I’m not an expert, it looks as though the archeological evidence disfavors the hypothesis that the Conquest of Canaan occurred. Ai, for example, was unoccupied during the supposed conquest period, and Jericho didn’t have walls at the relevant time.

11 Conclusion

I won’t comment on the rest of the book, as it’s largely about Pascal’s wager (where my thoughts are unique, and best discussed in another article) and the problem of divine hiddenness. Overall, I found the book to be a good presentation of the case for being a relatively mainstream, conservative Christian.

This is not the kind of Christianity I find most plausible. If I were to become Christian, I would think the Bible had errors and the slaughter of the Canaanites and Amalekites didn’t really occur. In sum, then, I am not very moved by the major positive arguments in favor of Christianity, and I find the arguments against inerrancy very strong.

I recommend the book if you want to show someone the case in brief for Christianity—combined with a vivid description of how epic the Christian story is. The book is also a very fun read. But in the end, I am not moved by its central arguments for Christianity and remain, for now at least, unconvinced.

From this article here I find the following quotes about the grub:

There is more to this insect however as we look at the life-cycle of the mother:

  • The mother climbs up a piece of wood, mainly a particular type of tree, in order to lay her eggs

  • She then attaches herself to the tree building a hard red shell around her.

  • Inside this crimson shell she lays her eggs and keeps them under her body to protect them.

  • The baby grubs are hatched and they feed on the mother’s body for 3 days.

  • During this time a bright crimson red fluid oozes from the mother.

  • This red fluid stains the wood that she is attached to and the baby grubs are covered being permanently stained with it.

  • The young are ready to leave the shell after 3 days.

  • The mother, being still attached to the shell and to the tree, dies so that she can birth a family.

  • On day 4 the mother’s tail pulls up to her head making a heart-like shape and she is no longer red – she has turned into a snow-white wax.

  • This snow-white body looks like a little piece of wool on the side of the tree. It begins to flake off and falls to the ground like snow.

I asked Claude to fact check. Here was its reply:

The page’s claims, one by one

  1. She climbs a particular tree and attaches herself. Roughly true. She’s immobile as an adult; it’s the crawler that walks. One host-plant genus, so “particular tree” is fair.

  2. Builds a hard red shell. Half true. Hard and shell-like, yes. Red, no — gray-brown externally.

  3. Lays eggs under her body for protection. True, or near enough; she retains them and the crawlers emerge from beneath her.

  4. The grubs feed on the mother’s body for three days. False. No source in the entomological literature describes this. They emerge, disperse, and go dormant; their first meal is oak sap months later.

  5. Crimson fluid oozes from her during this period. False. The pigment is intracellular; dye is obtained by drying and crushing harvested insects. The Oklahoma extension description of a congeneric Kermes explicitly has crawlers emerging “from beneath the mother’s scale covering” with no mention of any fluid.

  6. It stains the wood and the grubs are permanently stained. False / unsupported. The nymphs are red because they contain the pigment, not because they’re painted with it.

  7. The young leave after three days. Not attested. Crawler emergence spans weeks across a population.

  8. The mother dies, still attached. True.

  9. On day four her tail curls to her head in a heart shape and she turns snow-white like wax. False. Dead females are described as sclerotized globose shells, sometimes with parasitoid exit holes. No color change to white is reported anywhere.

  10. The white body flakes off and falls like snow. False / unsupported.

So basically it looks like there’s an insect that gets on a tree, makes a brown shell, protects her grubs, and dies. This is not an impressive parallel of Jesus.

item.title: Extreme Vegan Claims Aren’t Hyperbole
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

The perception that lots of people have of vegans is that we’re a group unusually prone to hyperbole. While you try to eat your hamburger in peace, we start screeching about gas chambers, rape, torture, and murder. Can’t we just leave you alone? And why do we need to make such extreme claims all the time?

The fact that a group is making extreme claims doesn’t tell you if those claims are correct. The quantum physicists say all sorts of nutty things, but their claims are correct. You need to figure out if the extreme claims are justified. In my view, most extreme claims that are made by vegans are correct. Animal farming is depraved enough that accurate descriptions sound like outrageous hyperbole.

For example, vegans commonly claim that meat production involves torture. This is an outrageous and scandalous claim. It also happens to be true. Animals routinely undergo conditions that we’d all agree were torture if you did them to a dog. For example, they’re often locked in tiny cages where they can’t turn around.

If someone locked a puppy in a cage for its whole life, it would be reasonable to say they were torturing the puppy. Similarly, if after doing this, they cut off the puppies’ fingers without anesthetic and burned it with a hot iron, calling this torture would not be outrageous hyperbole. It would be accurate. But all this things are routine in the animal farming industry.

Some of the widespread practices that are reasonably called torture:

  • Grinding up baby chicks in shredders. This happens to billions of them every year.

  • Suffocating fish to death (after starving them for several days).

  • Selectively breeding animals to be barely able to walk.

  • Locking them in tiny cages where they can’t turn around.

  • Sending them into transport trucks so that a huge fraction of them break bones.

  • Systematically starving millions of egg-laying hens to boost egg production.

  • Disbudding with a ~600 degree iron.

  • Debeaking.

  • Branding.

These were just examples from memory—many more examples could be given. And these describe ordinary industry practices. If one accounts for what happens when ordinary practice is not followed—say, when a million birds are boiled alive every year, or when a chicken’s foot is ripped off, or when tails are torn off slowly with dull pliers, or when workers hit and kick animals as they do routinely—then torture is even more common and extreme.

Or, to take another example, vegans talk a lot about murdering animals. People think this is outrageous. But if I shot a puppy in cold blood for no reason, few would think it was outrageous to describe it as murder. So if we kill animals by the billions, despite not needing to, and torture them as well, then this is accurately described as murder.

Why do we talk about gas chambers so much? The answer is that animals are often killed or stunned in gas chambers. I recommend watching videos of it if you deny that it’s a horrific experience for the animals.

Why do we talk about rape? Because the conditions animals undergo are ones that you’d call rape if someone did them to a human. For example, this is what’s done to turkeys (similar things are done to cows):

The hens weigh 20 to 30 pounds and are terrified, beating their wings and struggling in panic. They go through this every week for more than a year, and they don’t like it. Once you have grabbed her with one hand, you flop her down chest first on the edge of the pit with the tail end sticking up. You put your free hand over the vent and tail and pull the rump and tail feathers upward. At the same time, you pull the hand holding the feet downward, thus “breaking” the hen so that her rear is straight up and her vent open. The inseminator sticks his thumb right under the vent and pushes, which opens it further until the end of the oviduct is exposed. Into this, he inserts a straw of semen connected to the end of a tube from an air compressor and pulls a trigger, releasing a shot of compressed air that blows the semen solution from the straw and into the hen’s oviduct. Then you let go of the hen and she flops away.

If you hold a creature down and inject it with semen against its will, we would call this rape in other contexts. Or, at the very least, we’d consider it a serious kind of sexual assault. So it is alarming that we do this to so many animals.

Here’s the most outrageous claim of all: animals experience more suffering in a few years of factory farming than all the suffering of human history. If you torture tens of billions of beings in the most horrendous conditions imaginable, so that in two years a population of land animals is slaughtered that surpasses the number of humans that have ever lived, and more than one order of magnitude more sea creatures are killed than land animals, then the above claim is very plausible. If animals can suffer, as overwhelming evidence indicates they can, the cry going out from the factory farms is loud enough to to drown out all the cries in human history.

The animals that are being tortured by the hundreds of billions are, with respect to their mental capacities, like very mentally disabled humans. Insofar as their suffering matters due to how it feels, as ours does, then factory farming is worse than all the suffering in human history.

These are, as I say, outrageous and incredible claims. But sometimes outrageous things are true. We should direct our outrage at the factory farms that do these wicked things, rather than at the people who point them out.

item.title: The Vindication of Normal Politics
item.description: SLOW BORING HAS BEEN VINDICATED AT THE BALLOT BOX
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Democrats had a pretty good night!

Historically good, in fact. There was a +14.5 point swing relative to 2024 in the Senate. As of the time I’m writing this, there is, amazingly, uncertainty about who is going to win Mississippi. And Democrats are the favorites! We also won Kansas! Not only have Democrats won Texas and North Carolina, they’ve done so by huge margins. Talarico beat Paxton by around 11 points.

Now, part of the explanation of Talarico’s victory was that Paxton was some kind of swamp creature dredged up from the local morgue. But even Abbott was defeated by more than seven points in a race that was thought to be an easy lock for Republicans.

A very common phenomenon in politics is when political commentators suggest that their preferred candidate isn’t just better on the issues but would be electorally better. There is a suspicious convergence between how people think the country ought to be run and what policies are best for electoral victories. I like to think I don’t do that—for example, though I share Hillary Clinton’s political views a lot more than Bernie Sanders’, I think Bernie would have done better against Trump in 2016.

So I hope I’ve built up some credibility when I say that this election is good evidence that my preferred candidates are the ones that the parties should run.

I’m a moderate liberal (well, I have some extreme views, as you may know, but they’re not within the political Overton window). I prefer candidates who are moderate and hinged. I think the 2012-era Republican party is vastly preferable to the current one. Similarly, I like when Democrats run fairly moderate candidates. Politics was peak in the Obama vs. Romney years and has gone disastrously downhill since then.

So which candidates did best? This chart, courtesy of , is a good indicator of the candidates who performed best relative to the average D+14.5 swing.

The candidates who did best are mostly moderates. Democrats in red states tended to be more moderate on average, and they hugely overperformed. For example, in North Carolina, Roy Cooper sailed to an easy victory by nearly 20 points, running on the slogan “make stuff cost less.” Progressives like Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan underperformed. As Yglesias notes:

The real ideological fuckup was in ME-2, the only House seat that flipped from blue to red, where Democrats replaced Jared Golden with Bernie-endorsed Matt Dunlap, who lost despite a huge blue wave.

The Trumpian Republican party is very unpopular right now. So in races that were a referendum on Trump, Democrats won easily. In races that were a referendum on a more controversial progressive agenda—well, Democrats still won, because they basically won everywhere by a million points, but it was a lot closer. They won by only 52 points, rather than 85. The model of the future is: be a normal kind of chill moderate who runs on a slogan like “make stuff cost less.”

This election is also about as strong a rebuke of Trumpism as you can get. The Republican who most overperformed in the senate is Susan Collins. In fact, she did better than Republicans did in 2024! She still lost, but did extremely well. Collins is one of the most moderate Republicans—and the ones least friendly to Trump. Collins is, in many respects, a faint echo of the pre-Trump Republican party.

There is a perfectly sensible explanation of this. Trump is a deeply unpopular president because he tanked the global economy through unpopular and voluntary actions—both tariffs and the war in Iran—and then ran the presidency as some kind of demented and corrupt clown show. For example, in the run-up to the midterms, he decided to talk extensively about the Lincoln Memorial’s reflecting pool. This was…a choice.

It is bad for your political fortunes to go from a House, Senate, presidency trifecta into the midterms. It is especially bad if the economy is doing badly and gas prices are up. It is especially especially bad if the economic woes are the straightforward result of unpopular policies enacted by the president. And if on top of this, the president seems to be treating the reflecting pool and White House Ballroom as the central issue of the election, then that is a recipe for a historic shellacking.

Matt Yglesias’s blog is titled Slow Boring, a reference to the Max Weber quote “Politics is a strong and slow boring of hard boards.” Last night was a good night for slow boring politics. Voters aren’t happy with reckless unilateralism, and while very progressive Democrats still won by a considerable margin, they won by a lot less than their more moderate compatriots. The fact that the tariffs played a role in the humongous midterms defeat is further vindication of the Slow Boring worldview—according to which you shouldn’t ignore what one learns in Econ 101!

The model of the future for the Democrats is to run candidates like Jon Ossoff, Roy Cooper, and Josh Shapiro. The model of the future, if we want to win elections, is slow and boring. The insanity and the clown show has been decisively repudiated. Slow Boring has been vindicated!
